meaning: Enter your account using your name and password.
easyEnglish: Enter your account using your name and password.
japanese: アカウントにログインする。
cue: You cannot see your saved files because you have not entered your account. Explain what you need to do.
reply: I need to log in before I can open my files.
transferCue: A colleague asks how to access the team calendar. Tell them to use their work account.
transferReply: Log in with your work email to see the shared calendar.
frame: log in / log in to an account
nuance: The verb is two words. Login can be a noun, as in a login page. Keep the account after to.

meaning: Record your arrival or enter an online account.
easyEnglish: Record your arrival or enter an online account.
japanese: 到着を記録する、またはオンラインのアカウントに入る。
cue: You are visiting an office. Ask whether you need to record your arrival.
reply: Do I need to sign in at reception?
transferCue: A guest wants to use the building's Wi-Fi. Explain the first step.
transferReply: You can sign in with the code on your visitor pass.
frame: sign in / sign in at a place
nuance: At a building, signing in records your arrival. Online, it can mean entering an account.

meaning: Leave an online account so it is no longer open.
easyEnglish: Leave an online account so it is no longer open.
japanese: オンラインのアカウントからサインアウトする。
cue: Your friend has finished using email on a shared computer. Remind them to close their account.
reply: Remember to sign out before you leave the computer.
transferCue: You are about to lend someone your tablet. Explain why you need a moment.
transferReply: I'll sign out of my account first, then you can use it.
frame: sign out / sign out of an account
nuance: Keep of before the account. Closing a browser window does not always sign you out.

meaning: Connect a device to an electricity supply or another device.
easyEnglish: Connect a device to an electricity supply or another device.
japanese: 機器のプラグを電源や別の機器につなぐ。
cue: Your phone battery is nearly empty. Ask to use a nearby socket.
reply: Can I plug my phone in here?
transferCue: A colleague cannot hear sound through their headset. Suggest checking the connection.
transferReply: Try plugging the headset in again.
frame: plug something in / plug it in
nuance: Separable: plug it in. Use into before a named socket or port: plug it into this port.

meaning: Make a light or machine start working with its control.
easyEnglish: Make a light or machine start working with its control.
japanese: スイッチを入れて、照明や機械をつける。
cue: The room is dark. Offer to turn on the light.
reply: I'll switch the light on so we can see.
transferCue: Your guest is cold. Tell them how to use the heater.
transferReply: You can switch it on with this button.
frame: switch something on / switch it on
nuance: Separable. Switch on and turn on are often interchangeable for lights and appliances.

meaning: Make a light or machine stop working with its control.
easyEnglish: Make a light or machine stop working with its control.
japanese: スイッチを切って、照明や機械を消す。
cue: Everyone is leaving the meeting room. Remind them about the projector.
reply: Could someone switch the projector off?
transferCue: A fan is making it hard to hear. Ask your friend to stop it.
transferReply: Could you switch it off while we're talking?
frame: switch something off / switch it off
nuance: Separable. This entry teaches stopping a device; switch off can also mean mentally stop paying attention.

meaning: Stop a supply or stop a machine from operating.
easyEnglish: Stop a supply or stop a machine from operating.
japanese: 供給を止める、機械を停止させる。
cue: A pipe is leaking. Explain what you will do before calling for help.
reply: I'll shut off the water and call the building manager.
transferCue: You are describing a coffee machine's safety feature.
transferReply: It shuts off automatically after an hour.
frame: shut something off / something shuts off
nuance: Can be transitive or intransitive. Often used for water, gas, power or automatic equipment.

meaning: Put electrical energy into a battery.
easyEnglish: Put electrical energy into a battery.
japanese: バッテリーを充電する。
cue: You are going on a long walk and your phone is nearly empty. Explain the delay.
reply: I need to charge my phone up before we leave.
transferCue: A friend asks whether the camera is ready for tomorrow.
transferReply: I've charged it up, so we're ready to go.
frame: charge something up / charge it up
nuance: Separable. Charge is also common without up; up emphasizes getting the battery ready to use.

meaning: Make a computer or machine begin operating.
easyEnglish: Make a computer or machine begin operating.
japanese: コンピューターや機械を起動する。
cue: A coworker asks why you are not ready to share your screen.
reply: My computer is still starting up.
transferCue: You are opening a workshop. Say what you will do first.
transferReply: I'll start the machines up while you check the orders.
frame: start something up / something starts up
nuance: Can be transitive or intransitive. The noun startup, meaning a new business, is a separate use.

meaning: Remove dirt or mess from a place.
easyEnglish: Remove dirt or mess from a place.
japanese: 汚れや散らかったものを片づけて、きれいにする。
cue: Your friends have cooked dinner. Offer to deal with the kitchen afterward.
reply: You cooked, so I'll clean up the kitchen.
transferCue: A drink spills across a table. Reassure your guest.
transferReply: Don't worry. I'll clean it up.
frame: clean something up / clean it up
nuance: Separable. Clean up emphasizes dealing with a mess; tidy up focuses on putting things in order.

meaning: Put things in their proper places so a room looks neat.
easyEnglish: Put things in their proper places so a room looks neat.
japanese: 物を所定の場所に戻して、部屋を整える。
cue: A friend is arriving soon and your room is messy. Explain what you are doing.
reply: I'm tidying up before my friend arrives.
transferCue: You need space on a desk to work. Ask someone to organize it.
transferReply: Could you tidy the desk up a little?
nuance: Can be used without an object. Tidying does not necessarily involve washing or removing dirt.

meaning: Remove something from a surface using water.
easyEnglish: Remove something from a surface using water.
japanese: 水で洗って、表面についているものを落とす。
cue: You have mud on your hands after gardening. Say what you will do.
reply: I'll wash the mud off before I come inside.
transferCue: Your friend has paint on their arm. Suggest using soap.
transferReply: Try washing it off with soap and warm water.
frame: wash something off / wash it off
nuance: Separable. Use off to show removal from a surface, not cleaning a whole room.

meaning: Remove something from a surface with a cloth or your hand.
easyEnglish: Remove something from a surface with a cloth or your hand.
japanese: 布や手で拭いて、表面についているものを落とす。
cue: There are crumbs on the table. Offer to remove them.
reply: I'll wipe the crumbs off before we eat.
transferCue: Someone has spilled coffee on a counter. Hand them a cloth and make a request.
transferReply: Could you wipe it off with this cloth?
frame: wipe something off / wipe it off
nuance: Separable. Wipe describes the action; off emphasizes removing what is on the surface.

meaning: Remove water from your body or another wet surface.
easyEnglish: Remove water from your body or another wet surface.
japanese: 体や物についた水を拭くなどして乾かす。
cue: You have just left a swimming pool. Ask for a towel.
reply: Can I borrow a towel to dry off?
transferCue: Your dog has been out in the rain. Explain what you will do before letting it on the sofa.
transferReply: I'll dry him off first.
frame: dry off / dry someone or something off
nuance: Can be intransitive or separable. Dry up often describes a supply disappearing, which is a different sense.

meaning: Become unavailable after there used to be a supply.
easyEnglish: Become unavailable after there used to be a supply.
japanese: 資金や仕事などの供給が途絶える。
cue: A project has lost its funding. Explain why work stopped.
reply: The funding dried up, so we had to pause the project.
transferCue: You are worried that freelance jobs are becoming scarce.
transferReply: If the work dries up, I'll look for a part-time job.
nuance: In this figurative sense, the subject is often money, work or information. It can also describe water disappearing.

meaning: Remove soap or dirt with clean water.
easyEnglish: Remove soap or dirt with clean water.
japanese: きれいな水ですすいで、泡や汚れを落とす。
cue: There is soap left on a plate. Ask someone to remove it.
reply: Could you rinse the soap off this plate?
transferCue: You have been swimming in the sea. Say what you will do at the shower.
transferReply: I'll rinse off before I get dressed.
nuance: Can be separable or used without an object. Rinse emphasizes using water after washing or swimming.

meaning: Put your things into bags or containers when you are leaving.
easyEnglish: Put your things into bags or containers when you are leaving.
japanese: 帰るために荷物をまとめる。
cue: It is nearly time to leave a picnic. Suggest putting everything away.
reply: Let's pack up before it gets dark.
transferCue: Your coworker asks when you will be ready to leave.
transferReply: I'm just packing my things up. I'll be ready in a minute.
nuance: Separable when there is an object. This entry teaches gathering belongings, not a machine breaking down.

meaning: Lock the doors of a place before leaving it.
easyEnglish: Lock the doors of a place before leaving it.
japanese: その場を離れる前に戸締まりをする。
cue: You are the last person leaving a shop. Offer to secure it.
reply: I'll lock up after everyone has left.
transferCue: Your flatmate is leaving after you. Remind them about the doors.
transferReply: Could you lock the house up when you go?
frame: lock up / lock a place up
nuance: Can be used without an object. Lock someone up, meaning imprison them, is a different use.

meaning: Prevent someone from entering a place or account.
easyEnglish: Prevent someone from entering a place or account.
japanese: 人が建物やアカウントに入れない状態にする。
cue: You left your keys inside and the door has closed. Explain the problem.
reply: I've locked myself out of the apartment.
transferCue: You entered your password incorrectly several times. Explain why you need support.
transferReply: The system has locked me out of my account.
frame: lock someone out / be locked out of something
nuance: Separable: lock me out. Keep of before the place or account that cannot be entered.

meaning: Visit someone or a place for a short time.
easyEnglish: Visit someone or a place for a short time.
japanese: 人や場所をちょっと訪ねる、立ち寄る。
cue: You will be near a friend's home tomorrow. Ask about a short visit.
reply: Could I stop by tomorrow afternoon?
transferCue: Your colleague needs a signed form. Say when you will visit their desk.
transferReply: I'll stop by your desk after lunch.
frame: stop by / stop by a place
nuance: Usually suggests a short, informal visit. A place can follow by directly.

meaning: Make a short stop somewhere during a journey.
easyEnglish: Make a short stop somewhere during a journey.
japanese: 移動の途中で短時間立ち寄る。
cue: You are driving to a friend's home and need food. Suggest a stop on the way.
reply: Let's stop off at a shop on the way.
transferCue: Someone asks why your journey took longer than expected.
transferReply: We stopped off for a coffee before continuing.
frame: stop off at a place / stop off for something
nuance: Emphasizes a stop within a longer journey. Stop over often involves staying somewhere longer, especially overnight.

meaning: Stay somewhere briefly during a longer journey.
easyEnglish: Stay somewhere briefly during a longer journey.
japanese: 長い旅の途中で、ある場所に短く滞在する。
cue: You are describing a flight with an overnight break in another city.
reply: We're stopping over in Singapore for one night.
transferCue: A friend asks whether you will travel straight home.
transferReply: I might stop over in Dubai on the way back.
nuance: Common in travel. The noun stopover is one word; the verb stop over is two.

meaning: Spend time at home instead of going out.
easyEnglish: Spend time at home instead of going out.
japanese: 外出せず家で過ごす。
cue: Your friends suggest going out, but you need a quiet evening.
reply: I think I'll stay in tonight.
transferCue: The weather forecast is bad. Suggest an indoor plan for the evening.
transferReply: Let's stay in and cook something together.
nuance: No direct object in this sense. Stay out describes the opposite choice.

meaning: Remain away from home, often late into the evening.
easyEnglish: Remain away from home, often late into the evening.
japanese: 家に帰らず外で過ごす。
cue: Your flatmate asks whether you will be home for dinner.
reply: I'm going to stay out a bit later tonight.
transferCue: You have an early start tomorrow. Explain why you want to leave a party.
transferReply: I can't stay out too late. I have an early train.
nuance: No direct object in this sense. Stay out of something, meaning avoid involvement, is a different construction.

meaning: Sleep at someone else's home for a night.
easyEnglish: Sleep at someone else's home for a night.
japanese: 人の家に一晩泊まる。
cue: A friend has missed the last train. Offer them a place to sleep.
reply: You can stay over if you like.
transferCue: You are arranging a weekend visit. Ask whether you can spend the night.
transferReply: Would it be okay if I stayed over on Saturday?
frame: stay over / stay over at someone's place
nuance: Usually refers to an overnight visit, not moving in permanently.

meaning: Avoid going near a person or place.
easyEnglish: Avoid going near a person or place.
japanese: 人や場所に近づかない。
cue: A floor has just been painted. Warn someone not to go near it.
reply: Please stay away from that area until the paint dries.
transferCue: You need quiet to finish a project. Explain how you will avoid distractions.
transferReply: I'm staying away from social media this afternoon.
frame: stay away from someone or something
nuance: Keep from before the person, place or activity being avoided.

meaning: Move to the side to make room for someone.
easyEnglish: Move to the side to make room for someone.
japanese: 横にずれて、人のために場所を空ける。
cue: You want to sit next to a friend on a bench. Ask for some space.
reply: Could you move over a little?
transferCue: A colleague needs room at a shared table. Offer to make space.
transferReply: I'll move over so you can sit here.
nuance: Usually intransitive. Add a little to make a request less abrupt.

meaning: Change to a higher position or rank.
easyEnglish: Change to a higher position or rank.
japanese: より上の地位や段階に進む。
cue: A friend asks about your colleague's promotion.
reply: She's moved up to a team leader role.
transferCue: You want to develop your career within your current company.
transferReply: I'd like to move up in the company over the next few years.
frame: move up / move up to a position
nuance: This entry teaches advancement. Move a meeting up, meaning schedule it earlier, is a different use.

meaning: Return to live in a place where you lived before.
easyEnglish: Return to live in a place where you lived before.
japanese: 以前住んでいた場所に戻って暮らす。
cue: A friend asks why you are leaving your current city.
reply: I'm moving back to my hometown next month.
transferCue: You are talking about a friend's plans after studying abroad.
transferReply: He's decided to move back after graduation.
frame: move back / move back to a place
nuance: Keep to before the destination. Move something back can instead mean return an object to its earlier position.

meaning: Become involved to help or deal with a problem.
easyEnglish: Become involved to help or deal with a problem.
japanese: 問題に対処するために間に入る。
cue: A discussion is becoming an argument. Explain what the manager did.
reply: Our manager stepped in before it became a bigger problem.
transferCue: A colleague is struggling to finish a task. Offer help if needed.
transferReply: I can step in if you need another pair of hands.
frame: step in / step in to help
nuance: Usually intransitive. It often implies involvement at a moment when help or intervention is needed.

meaning: Leave a room or place for a short time.
easyEnglish: Leave a room or place for a short time.
japanese: 部屋やその場から少しの間外に出る。
cue: You need to take a private call during a meeting. Explain your brief absence.
reply: I need to step out for a quick call.
transferCue: Someone asks where a colleague has gone. Tell them the colleague will return soon.
transferReply: She's stepped out for a moment, but she'll be back soon.
frame: step out / step out for a moment
nuance: Often a polite way to describe a brief absence without giving much detail.

meaning: Leave a position so someone else can take it.
easyEnglish: Leave a position so someone else can take it.
japanese: 役職を退き、ほかの人に任せる。
cue: A team leader wants someone new to lead the project. Explain the decision.
reply: He's stepping aside so someone else can lead the next phase.
transferCue: You have led a club for years and want to let another member try.
transferReply: I think it's time for me to step aside.
frame: step aside / step aside as a leader
nuance: This sense concerns responsibility or leadership. It can also literally mean moving out of someone's way.

meaning: Pause your involvement to think about the whole situation.
easyEnglish: Pause your involvement to think about the whole situation.
japanese: いったん距離を置いて、状況全体を考える。
cue: Your team is arguing about a small detail. Suggest considering the bigger issue.
reply: Let's step back and think about what we're trying to achieve.
transferCue: You are too involved in a disagreement to judge it calmly.
transferReply: I need to step back from this for a day or two.
frame: step back / step back from something
nuance: Often figurative. It suggests gaining perspective, not necessarily leaving a role permanently.

meaning: Move into an upright sitting position.
easyEnglish: Move into an upright sitting position.
japanese: 上半身を起こして座る。
cue: A friend is lying on the sofa and wants a drink. Ask them to sit upright.
reply: Can you sit up so I can hand you the glass?
transferCue: You heard a noise while resting in bed. Describe your reaction.
transferReply: I sat up to see where the noise was coming from.
nuance: Intransitive in this sense. The exercise noun sit-up is different.

meaning: Put your body flat on a bed or another surface to rest.
easyEnglish: Put your body flat on a bed or another surface to rest.
japanese: 横になって休む。
cue: You feel tired after a long journey. Say what you need.
reply: I'd like to lie down for a few minutes.
transferCue: A friend has been on their feet all day. Suggest a rest.
transferReply: Why don't you lie down while I make some tea?
frame: lie down / lay down / lain down
nuance: Lie is intransitive here: lie down, not lie yourself down. Its past form is lay, not lied.

meaning: Rest with your back supported in a relaxed position.
easyEnglish: Rest with your back supported in a relaxed position.
japanese: 背中を預けて、楽な姿勢でもたれる。
cue: A friend is trying your reclining chair. Invite them to relax.
reply: Lie back and make yourself comfortable.
transferCue: You are describing a peaceful afternoon in the garden.
transferReply: We lay back in our chairs and watched the clouds.
frame: lie back / lay back / lain back
nuance: Lie is intransitive. Lay back is the past form here; lie back is the present form.

meaning: Rely on someone for support when things are difficult.
easyEnglish: Rely on someone for support when things are difficult.
japanese: 困っているとき、人を頼り支えてもらう。
cue: A friend feels they must handle a difficult time alone. Offer emotional support.
reply: You can lean on me if things get difficult.
transferCue: You are talking about the people who helped you after a move.
transferReply: I leaned on my friends a lot during those first few months.
nuance: Keep the person after on. Lean on can also mean pressure someone; this entry teaches relying on support.

meaning: Lower the upper part of your body toward the ground.
easyEnglish: Lower the upper part of your body toward the ground.
japanese: かがんで、上半身を地面に近づける。
cue: Your keys have fallen on the floor. Describe how you picked them up.
reply: I bent down to pick up my keys.
transferCue: You cannot reach something under a chair while standing. Ask a friend for help.
transferReply: Could you bend down and see if my bag is under the chair?
nuance: Usually followed by to and the purpose of the movement. Bent is the past form.

meaning: Move the upper part of your body forward and down.
easyEnglish: Move the upper part of your body forward and down.
japanese: 上半身を前に倒してかがむ。
cue: A doorway is very low. Warn a tall friend.
reply: You'll need to bend over to get through this doorway.
transferCue: You are describing how you tied your shoes.
transferReply: I bent over to tie my shoes before we left.
nuance: Intransitive in these examples. Bend something over can instead describe folding an object.

meaning: Lower yourself so one or both knees are on the ground.
easyEnglish: Lower yourself so one or both knees are on the ground.
japanese: ひざを地面につける。
cue: You want to speak to a small child at eye level. Explain what you did.
reply: I knelt down so we could talk face to face.
transferCue: You are looking for something beneath a sofa. Ask someone to help.
transferReply: Could you kneel down and look under the sofa?
frame: kneel down / knelt down or kneeled down
nuance: Both knelt and kneeled are accepted past forms. The movement ends with knees on the ground.

meaning: Move your hand toward something you want to take.
easyEnglish: Move your hand toward something you want to take.
japanese: 取ろうとして物に手を伸ばす。
cue: You nearly knocked over a glass while getting your phone. Explain what happened.
reply: I was reaching for my phone and almost hit the glass.
transferCue: A friend cannot get a book from a shelf. Describe their attempt.
transferReply: She reached for the book, but it was too high.
nuance: Keep the object after for. Reaching for something does not mean you successfully got it.

meaning: Leave a situation instead of staying involved.
easyEnglish: Leave a situation instead of staying involved.
japanese: 関わり続けず、その状況から離れる。
cue: An argument is getting worse. Say what you chose to do.
reply: I decided to walk away rather than keep arguing.
transferCue: A business deal feels wrong to you. Explain your choice.
transferReply: I'm prepared to walk away from the deal if the terms don't change.
frame: walk away / walk away from something
nuance: Can describe physically leaving or ending involvement. Keep from before the situation being left.

meaning: Reduce an unpleasant feeling by walking.
easyEnglish: Reduce an unpleasant feeling by walking.
japanese: 歩くことで不快感などを和らげる。
cue: You feel full after a big lunch. Suggest going for a walk.
reply: Let's walk off lunch before we get back in the car.
transferCue: You are annoyed after a call and need to calm down.
transferReply: I'm going outside to walk it off.
frame: walk something off / walk it off
nuance: Separable in this sense. Walk off without an object can simply mean leave on foot.

meaning: Explain or demonstrate each step of a process.
easyEnglish: Explain or demonstrate each step of a process.
japanese: 手順を一つずつ説明する、実演する。
cue: A new colleague does not know how to submit expenses. Offer guidance.
reply: I can walk you through the process.
transferCue: You do not understand a calculation in a report. Ask for a step-by-step explanation.
transferReply: Could you walk me through how you got that number?
nuance: Place the person after walk, then through and the process. A walkthrough can be a noun.

meaning: Become involved in an unpleasant situation without expecting it.
easyEnglish: Become involved in an unpleasant situation without expecting it.
japanese: 予想せず、困った状況に巻き込まれる。
cue: You joined a discussion without realizing people were arguing. Describe it.
reply: I walked into an argument without knowing what had happened.
transferCue: You nearly accepted a job with serious problems. Explain why you asked more questions.
transferReply: I wanted to know what I was walking into before I accepted.
nuance: Keep the situation after into. It often suggests lack of preparation or awareness.

meaning: Leave a place in a vehicle.
easyEnglish: Leave a place in a vehicle.
japanese: 車でその場を走り去る。
cue: A friend asks whether the taxi is still outside.
reply: No, it drove off a minute ago.
transferCue: Someone has left their bag behind. Ask the driver to wait.
transferReply: Wait! Don't drive off without my bag.
frame: drive off / drove off / driven off
nuance: Intransitive in this sense. Drive someone off, meaning force them away, is a different use.

meaning: Travel by car within an area, often without one direct route.
easyEnglish: Travel by car within an area, often without one direct route.
japanese: ある地域を車で走って回る。
cue: You could not find a parking space. Explain the delay.
reply: We drove around for twenty minutes looking for a space.
transferCue: You are visiting a new city. Suggest exploring by car.
transferReply: Let's drive around and see what the area is like.
frame: drive around / drive around an area
nuance: Round is a common British alternative to around. This entry concerns traveling within an area.

meaning: Arrive and stop in a vehicle, especially a train.
easyEnglish: Arrive and stop in a vehicle, especially a train.
japanese: 列車などが到着して止まる。
cue: You can see your friend's train arriving. Tell them where you are waiting.
reply: Your train is pulling in now. I'm near the front.
transferCue: You are describing when your bus arrived.
transferReply: The bus pulled in just as the rain started.
nuance: Intransitive. Pull out can describe leaving a station or moving out into traffic.

meaning: Stop being involved in an agreement or activity.
easyEnglish: Stop being involved in an agreement or activity.
japanese: 合意や活動への参加を取りやめる。
cue: A partner has decided not to continue with your project. Explain the change.
reply: Our partner has pulled out of the project.
transferCue: You agreed to an event but can no longer attend. Apologize for withdrawing.
transferReply: I'm sorry, but I have to pull out of the event.
frame: pull out / pull out of something
nuance: Keep of before the agreement or activity. The vehicle sense of pull out is different.

meaning: Start moving away in a vehicle.
easyEnglish: Start moving away in a vehicle.
japanese: 車や列車がその場を離れて動き出す。
cue: You reached the platform just as your train left. Describe the moment.
reply: The train was pulling away when I reached the platform.
transferCue: Someone is running toward your bus. Ask the driver to wait.
transferReply: Could you wait before you pull away? Someone's coming.
nuance: Intransitive in this sense. Often focuses on the first movement away from a stopping place.

meaning: Look or ask to make sure someone or something is okay.
easyEnglish: Look or ask to make sure someone or something is okay.
japanese: 人や物が大丈夫か確かめる。
cue: Your neighbor is unwell. Explain why you are going next door.
reply: I'm going to check on my neighbor.
transferCue: You left soup cooking in the kitchen. Ask someone to see whether it is ready.
transferReply: Could you check on the soup while I set the table?
nuance: Keep the object after on. Usually expresses concern or monitoring, rather than a detailed inspection.

meaning: Examine something to find mistakes or problems.
easyEnglish: Examine something to find mistakes or problems.
japanese: 間違いや問題がないか、ひと通り確認する。
cue: You have finished an email to a client. Ask a colleague to review it.
reply: Could you check this email over before I send it?
transferCue: You are buying a used bicycle. Explain what you want to do first.
transferReply: I'd like someone to check it over before I buy it.
frame: check something over / check it over
nuance: Separable. Check on asks whether things are okay; check over suggests examining the thing itself.

meaning: Mark an item on a list to show it is done or included.
easyEnglish: Mark an item on a list to show it is done or included.
japanese: リストの項目にチェックをつけて、完了や確認済みを示す。
cue: Your team is using a task list. Explain how to record completed work.
reply: Check each task off as you finish it.
transferCue: You are packing for a trip. Explain how you avoid forgetting things.
transferReply: I check things off on my packing list.
frame: check something off / check it off
nuance: Separable. Tick off is a common British alternative in this list-marking sense.

meaning: Temporarily do another person's work while they are away.
easyEnglish: Temporarily do another person's work while they are away.
japanese: 不在の人の代わりに、一時的に仕事をする。
cue: A colleague is away tomorrow. Offer to cover their role.
reply: I can fill in for Maya tomorrow.
transferCue: Your manager asks who handled the meeting while you were ill.
transferReply: Luis filled in for me at the meeting.
nuance: Keep the person after for. It describes temporary cover, unlike permanently taking over a role.

meaning: Accumulate a large bill or debt.
easyEnglish: Accumulate a large bill or debt.
japanese: 請求額や借金を積み上げる。
cue: Your mobile bill was high because of roaming. Explain what happened.
reply: I ran up a huge phone bill while I was abroad.
transferCue: You want to avoid spending too much on a credit card.
transferReply: I don't want to run up any more debt.
frame: run up a bill or debt / run it up
nuance: Often suggests a total growing through repeated spending. This is different from running toward someone.

meaning: Leave suddenly or quickly.
easyEnglish: Leave suddenly or quickly.
japanese: 急いでその場を立ち去る。
cue: You had to leave a conversation suddenly. Apologize to your friend.
reply: Sorry I ran off earlier. I had to catch my train.
transferCue: Your coworker is about to leave but you have one quick question.
transferReply: Before you run off, can I ask you something?
frame: run off / ran off / run off
nuance: Intransitive in this sense. Run off copies, meaning produce them, is a separate use.

meaning: Reach a person who is ahead of you.
easyEnglish: Reach a person who is ahead of you.
japanese: 先に進んでいる人に追いつく。
cue: Your friends are walking ahead while you tie your shoes. Tell them to continue.
reply: Go ahead. I'll catch up with you in a minute.
transferCue: You ran after your group at a station. Describe the result.
transferReply: I caught up with them near the ticket gates.
nuance: Keep the person after with. This entry teaches reaching someone, not exchanging news after a long time.

meaning: Go across a place to take a shorter route.
easyEnglish: Go across a place to take a shorter route.
japanese: 近道をするために場所を横切る。
cue: The road takes a long route around a park. Suggest a shortcut.
reply: We can cut across the park to get there faster.
transferCue: You arrived earlier than your friend expected. Explain your route.
transferReply: I cut across the square instead of following the main road.
nuance: Keep the place after across. Figuratively, cut across can also mean affect different groups or categories.

meaning: Go through a place to take a shorter route.
easyEnglish: Go through a place to take a shorter route.
japanese: 近道をするために場所を通り抜ける。
cue: You want to avoid walking around a large building. Suggest using a passage.
reply: Let's cut through the courtyard.
transferCue: Your friend asks how you got to the station so quickly.
transferReply: I cut through the shopping center.
nuance: Keep the place after through. This route sense differs from figurative uses such as cutting through confusion.

meaning: Use, eat or do less of something.
easyEnglish: Use, eat or do less of something.
japanese: 何かの使用量や摂取量、頻度を減らす。
cue: You want to drink less coffee in the evening. Explain your plan.
reply: I'm trying to cut down on coffee after lunch.
transferCue: Your team is spending too much time in meetings. Suggest a change.
transferReply: Could we cut down on meetings that don't need everyone?
nuance: Keep the object after on. It means reduce, rather than necessarily stop completely.

meaning: Reply to someone in a rude or challenging way.
easyEnglish: Reply to someone in a rude or challenging way.
japanese: 相手に失礼な態度で口答えする。
cue: You are describing why a child got into trouble at school.
reply: He got into trouble for talking back to the teacher.
transferCue: A friend thinks you were rude to a supervisor. Explain your intention.
transferReply: I wasn't trying to talk back. I just wanted to explain.
frame: talk back / talk back to someone
nuance: Often used when the other person has authority. The label can sound judgmental, so use it carefully.

meaning: Go away without taking someone or something with you.
easyEnglish: Go away without taking someone or something with you.
japanese: 人や物を置いて、その場を離れる。
cue: You realize your charger is still at a hotel. Explain what happened.
reply: I've left my charger behind at the hotel.
transferCue: Your group is leaving a busy market. Remind everyone to stay together.
transferReply: Let's make sure we don't leave anyone behind.
nuance: Separable: leave it behind. It may be accidental or deliberate; context tells you which.

meaning: Start a journey to a place.
easyEnglish: Start a journey to a place.
japanese: ある場所に向けて出発する。
cue: A friend asks when your trip starts.
reply: We're leaving for Nairobi on Friday.
transferCue: You are getting ready for work. Tell your flatmate when you will go.
transferReply: I need to leave for work in ten minutes.
nuance: Keep the destination after for. Leave a place names the place you depart from instead.

meaning: Start going toward the place you came from.
easyEnglish: Start going toward the place you came from.
japanese: もといた場所へ戻り始める。
cue: It is getting late during a day trip. Suggest returning.
reply: We should head back before it gets dark.
transferCue: A colleague asks where you are after a client visit.
transferReply: I'm heading back to the office now.
frame: head back / head back to a place
nuance: Keep to before a named destination, but say head back home without to.

meaning: Leave a place to go somewhere else.
easyEnglish: Leave a place to go somewhere else.
japanese: その場を出発する、出かける。
cue: You are about to leave home. Tell your flatmate.
reply: I'm heading out now. Do you need anything?
transferCue: Your group is ready to begin a walk. Suggest leaving.
transferReply: Shall we head out before it gets too hot?
frame: head out / head out for something
nuance: Informal and common in plans. Head out for lunch names the purpose of leaving.

meaning: Do something more quickly.
easyEnglish: Do something more quickly.
japanese: 急いで行動する。
cue: Your train leaves soon. Ask your friend to get ready faster.
reply: We need to hurry up or we'll miss the train.
transferCue: Someone is worried that they are keeping you waiting. Reassure them.
transferReply: You don't need to hurry up. We've got plenty of time.
nuance: A direct Hurry up! can sound impatient. We need to hurry up includes the speaker and often sounds softer.

meaning: Return quickly.
easyEnglish: Return quickly.
japanese: 急いで戻る。
cue: You need to go to a nearby shop while a friend waits. Promise a quick return.
reply: I'll hurry back so we can start the film.
transferCue: A colleague has an appointment before your presentation. Ask them to return in time.
transferReply: Could you hurry back? We need you for the first part.
frame: hurry back / hurry back to a place
nuance: Usually intransitive. Keep to before a destination, except with home.

meaning: Start or decide something without enough thought.
easyEnglish: Start or decide something without enough thought.
japanese: 十分に考えず、急いで決めたり始めたりする。
cue: A friend wants to accept an offer immediately. Suggest taking time.
reply: You don't have to rush into a decision.
transferCue: You are explaining why you want to wait before signing a contract.
transferReply: I don't want to rush into something I might regret.
frame: rush into something / rush into doing something
nuance: Keep the decision or activity after into. Often suggests that more thought would be useful.

meaning: Do something too quickly to give it enough attention.
easyEnglish: Do something too quickly to give it enough attention.
japanese: 十分に注意を払わず、急いで済ませる。
cue: A colleague completed a report too quickly and missed errors. Explain the problem.
reply: I think we rushed through the final checks.
transferCue: You want enough time to discuss a proposal properly.
transferReply: Let's not rush through this part. It's an important decision.
nuance: Keep the activity after through. The context often implies that speed reduces care.

meaning: Stand in a line while waiting for something.
easyEnglish: Stand in a line while waiting for something.
japanese: 順番を待って列に並ぶ。
cue: You see people waiting outside a bakery. Explain what they are doing.
reply: They're queuing up for fresh bread.
transferCue: A friend asks whether you can enter a museum immediately.
transferReply: We need to queue up for tickets first.
frame: queue up / queue up for something
nuance: Especially common in British English. Line up is widely used in American English. Both queuing and queueing occur.

meaning: Form or join a line of people waiting.
easyEnglish: Form or join a line of people waiting.
japanese: 人の列を作る、列に並ぶ。
cue: Visitors are entering a venue. Ask them to wait in a line.
reply: Please line up by the entrance.
transferCue: You arrived early for an event. Explain where you waited.
transferReply: We lined up outside before the doors opened.
frame: line up / line up for something
nuance: This entry teaches waiting in a line. Line something up can also mean arrange it for the future.

meaning: Take part in something other people are already doing.
easyEnglish: Take part in something other people are already doing.
japanese: ほかの人がしている活動に加わる。
cue: Your friends are playing a game. Ask whether you can take part.
reply: Can I join in?
transferCue: A new colleague is quiet during a group activity. Invite them to participate.
transferReply: You're welcome to join in whenever you're ready.
frame: join in / join in an activity
nuance: Join in focuses on participation. Join someone or join a club uses join without in.

meaning: Go with someone, often without being part of the original plan.
easyEnglish: Go with someone, often without being part of the original plan.
japanese: もとの予定には入っていなくても、人について行く。
cue: Your friends are visiting a market. Ask whether you can go too.
reply: Would you mind if I tagged along?
transferCue: Someone asks whether you organized the outing. Explain your role.
transferReply: I didn't plan it. I just tagged along with some friends.
frame: tag along / tag along with someone
nuance: Informal. It can suggest being an extra companion, so ask rather than assume you are invited.

meaning: Meet someone, usually by arrangement and socially.
easyEnglish: Meet someone, usually by arrangement and socially.
japanese: 約束して人と会う、待ち合わせる。
cue: You want to see a friend after work. Suggest a plan.
reply: Do you want to meet up after work?
transferCue: Your friends ask where the group should gather before dinner.
transferReply: Let's meet up outside the station at six.
frame: meet up / meet up with someone
nuance: Often informal and social. Keep with before the person: meet up with them.

meaning: Work together with another person or group.
easyEnglish: Work together with another person or group.
japanese: 人やグループと協力して取り組む。
cue: Two teams have similar goals. Suggest working together.
reply: We could team up to organize the event.
transferCue: You are explaining who helped you complete a project.
transferReply: I teamed up with a designer to build the first version.
frame: team up / team up with someone
nuance: Keep with before the partner and to before the purpose. Usually suggests cooperation on a shared task.

meaning: Form groups of two people.
easyEnglish: Form groups of two people.
japanese: 二人組になる。
cue: You are starting a workshop activity. Give the first instruction.
reply: Please pair up with someone you haven't worked with yet.
transferCue: A colleague asks how you will review the reports.
transferReply: We can pair up and check each other's work.
frame: pair up / pair up with someone
nuance: Usually used for an activity. Pair people up is also possible when someone organizes the pairs.

meaning: Go to bed for the night.
easyEnglish: Go to bed for the night.
japanese: 夜、寝床に入る。
cue: You are tired and want to end an evening conversation.
reply: I think I'll turn in. It's been a long day.
transferCue: A friend asks whether you want to watch another episode.
transferReply: I'll turn in early tonight. I have to be up at six.
nuance: Informal and intransitive in this sense. Turn something in, meaning submit it, is a different use.

meaning: Stop supporting someone and begin opposing them.
easyEnglish: Stop supporting someone and begin opposing them.
japanese: 支持していた人に反対するようになる。
cue: A leader has broken a promise. Describe the change in supporters' attitudes.
reply: Some of her supporters have turned against her.
transferCue: You worry that a disagreement is dividing your group.
transferReply: I don't want this argument to make us turn against each other.
nuance: Keep the object after against. It suggests a change from a previous relationship of support.

meaning: Become comfortable in a new home, job or situation.
easyEnglish: Become comfortable in a new home, job or situation.
japanese: 新しい住まいや仕事、環境になじむ。
cue: A colleague has just joined your team. Ask how they are adjusting.
reply: Are you settling in okay?
transferCue: You have recently moved. Explain why you have not invited friends over yet.
transferReply: We're still settling in, but we'd love to have you over soon.
frame: settle in / settle in at a new place
nuance: Focuses on adjustment after arrival. Settle down can instead mean begin a more stable way of life.

meaning: Pay the money you owe someone.
easyEnglish: Pay the money you owe someone.
japanese: 借りているお金や未払い分を精算する。
cue: A friend paid for your meal. Offer to pay your share.
reply: Let's settle up before we leave.
transferCue: You owe a colleague money for tickets. Ask when to repay them.
transferReply: Can I settle up with you tomorrow?
frame: settle up / settle up with someone
nuance: Informal. Usually concerns clearing an amount owed, often after a shared expense.

meaning: Spend less money on a particular expense.
easyEnglish: Spend less money on a particular expense.
japanese: ある費用を節約する。
cue: You share an apartment with a friend. Explain one reason for the arrangement.
reply: Sharing a place helps us save on rent.
transferCue: Your team wants to reduce printing costs. Suggest using digital documents.
transferReply: We could save on paper by sending the notes digitally.
nuance: Keep the expense after on. Save up means gradually collect money for a future purpose instead.

meaning: Put money into a bank account.
easyEnglish: Put money into a bank account.
japanese: 銀行口座にお金を預け入れる。
cue: You have cash from a sale. Explain why you are going to the bank.
reply: I need to pay this cash in.
transferCue: A friend asks what you did with a cheque.
transferReply: I paid it in at the bank this morning.
frame: pay money in / pay it in
nuance: Especially British English. Deposit is a common alternative. Use into before the account name.

meaning: Pay an amount of money, especially as an organization.
easyEnglish: Pay an amount of money, especially as an organization.
japanese: 組織などがまとまったお金を支払う。
cue: Your insurance claim has been accepted. Describe the result.
reply: The insurer paid out enough to cover the repairs.
transferCue: Your business has spent a lot on maintenance. Explain where the money went.
transferReply: We've paid out a lot for repairs this year.
frame: pay out money / pay money out
nuance: Separable. Often used for insurance, prizes, compensation or substantial expenses.

meaning: Say written words aloud so others can hear them.
easyEnglish: Say written words aloud so others can hear them.
japanese: 書いてある内容を声に出して読む。
cue: You cannot see a message on a colleague's screen. Ask them to say it aloud.
reply: Could you read the message out?
transferCue: You are leading a meeting. Explain how you will share the names of volunteers.
transferReply: I'll read out the names, then we can split into groups.
frame: read something out / read it out
nuance: Separable. The past form is spelled read but pronounced like red.

meaning: Prepare a complete written account using notes or information.
easyEnglish: Prepare a complete written account using notes or information.
japanese: メモや情報をもとに、まとまった文章に仕上げる。
cue: You have finished interviewing a customer. Explain your next task.
reply: I'll write up the interview notes this afternoon.
transferCue: Your team needs a record of a discussion. Volunteer to prepare it.
transferReply: I can write it up and share it with everyone tomorrow.
frame: write something up / write it up
nuance: Separable. Write down records information; write up develops it into an organized account.

meaning: Produce a paper copy of a digital document.
easyEnglish: Produce a paper copy of a digital document.
japanese: デジタル文書を紙に印刷する。
cue: Your phone may run out of battery during a trip. Explain how you will keep your ticket available.
reply: I'll print my ticket out before I leave.
transferCue: A colleague needs paper copies for a workshop. Offer to help.
transferReply: I can print them out for the group.
frame: print something out / print it out
nuance: Separable. Printout is a noun for the paper copy; print out is the verb.

meaning: Show a story or situation by performing it.
easyEnglish: Show a story or situation by performing it.
japanese: 場面や物語を演じて見せる。
cue: Your language class wants to practise ordering food. Suggest a role-play.
reply: Let's act out a conversation in a busy restaurant.
transferCue: Your nephew cannot explain a scene from a film. Offer another way.
transferReply: You could act it out and let us guess the film.
frame: Act something out / act it out
nuance: Separable. This lesson is about performing a scene; acting out can also mean behaving badly because of difficult feelings.

meaning: Include something extra in a price, list or plan.
easyEnglish: Include something extra in a price, list or plan.
japanese: 料金や項目などを追加する。
cue: A repair quote does not include delivery. Check the final price.
reply: Will you add on a delivery charge?
transferCue: A friend wants one more stop on your trip. Agree with a condition.
transferReply: We can add it on if we leave earlier.
frame: Add something on / add it on
nuance: Separable. Use two words for the verb; an add-on is an extra feature or item.

meaning: Stop light or sound from reaching you.
easyEnglish: Stop light or sound from reaching you.
japanese: 光や音などを遮る。
cue: Streetlights keep your room bright at night. Explain your new curtains.
reply: These curtains block out most of the light.
transferCue: A colleague asks why you wear headphones while writing.
transferReply: They help me block out the noise from the corridor.
frame: Block something out / block it out
nuance: Separable. This physical sense differs from deliberately avoiding a memory or reserving time in a calendar.

meaning: Become less serious and eventually end.
easyEnglish: Become less serious and eventually end.
japanese: 騒ぎや口論が収まる。
cue: A friend worries that one awkward remark has ruined a friendship. Offer perspective.
reply: The argument may blow over, but an apology would still help.
transferCue: Your team is waiting for public anger about a mistake to fade. Caution them.
transferReply: We can't just wait for this to blow over without fixing the problem.
frame: An argument blows over / wait for it to blow over
nuance: No direct object in this sense. It describes trouble fading; it does not mean the underlying problem has been solved.

meaning: Keep upsetting feelings inside instead of talking about them.
easyEnglish: Keep upsetting feelings inside instead of talking about them.
japanese: 感情や悩みを人に話さず、ため込む。
cue: A friend says they hide all their frustration. Offer to listen.
reply: You don't have to bottle up your feelings around me.
transferCue: Explain why you finally told your housemate what was bothering you.
transferReply: I kept bottling it up, and it was making things worse.
frame: Bottle something up / bottle it up
nuance: Separable. Usually used for feelings, anger or worries. An invitation to talk should leave the other person a choice.

meaning: Choose to leave a role or stop taking part.
easyEnglish: Choose to leave a role or stop taking part.
japanese: 役割や活動から身を引く。
cue: You have organized a club for years and want someone else to lead. Announce your decision.
reply: I'll bow out after this season and help the next organizer get started.
transferCue: You can no longer join a competition. Tell your partner.
transferReply: I need to bow out of the contest because of work.
frame: Bow out / bow out of something
nuance: No direct object. Often suggests a deliberate, fairly graceful departure. Bow here rhymes with how.

meaning: Begin to look or feel happier.
easyEnglish: Begin to look or feel happier.
japanese: 表情や気持ちが明るくなる。
cue: Describe your brother's reaction when an old friend called.
reply: He brightened up as soon as he heard her voice.
transferCue: A colleague seemed discouraged before seeing the first draft. Describe the change.
transferReply: She started to brighten up when she saw how much we'd finished.
nuance: Intransitive here. Brighten a room up instead means make it lighter or more cheerful.

meaning: Treat a concern or idea as unimportant without considering it properly.
easyEnglish: Treat a concern or idea as unimportant without considering it properly.
japanese: 意見や懸念をまともに取り合わない。
cue: Your safety concern was dismissed too quickly. Ask the team to reconsider.
reply: Please don't brush aside the reports from the evening staff.
transferCue: Describe why a colleague stopped offering suggestions.
transferReply: Her manager kept brushing her ideas aside.
frame: Brush something aside / brush it aside
nuance: Separable. Usually critical: the concern did not receive enough attention.

meaning: Accept an idea and believe that it is worth supporting.
easyEnglish: Accept an idea and believe that it is worth supporting.
japanese: 考えや計画を信じ、受け入れる。
cue: Your team suggests meetings alone will improve communication. Express doubt.
reply: I don't buy into the idea that more meetings always help.
transferCue: Explain why you agreed to a shared gardening project.
transferReply: I bought into the plan once I saw how the work would be shared.
frame: Buy into an idea / buy into it
nuance: Keep the idea after into. Can express either support or skepticism. Buying part of a business is another sense.

meaning: Build a place or role for yourself through effort.
easyEnglish: Build a place or role for yourself through effort.
japanese: 努力して自分の地位や役割を築く。
cue: A friend wants to know how a small studio survives among larger companies.
reply: They've carved out a niche making tools for local schools.
transferCue: Describe a designer who built a career without following a usual route.
transferReply: She carved out a career by working directly with small museums.
frame: Carve out a niche / carve out a career
nuance: Often used with niche, career or reputation. The sense is figurative; it emphasizes actively creating a place for yourself.

meaning: Cause someone to make a mistake or show that they were not prepared.
easyEnglish: Cause someone to make a mistake or show that they were not prepared.
japanese: 難しい点や予想外のことで人をつまずかせる。
cue: A colleague asks why a simple form took you so long.
reply: The date format caught me out; I put the month in the wrong box.
transferCue: A friend is preparing for an interview. Explain your practice questions.
transferReply: I'm not trying to catch you out. I just want you to feel prepared.
frame: Catch someone out / be caught out by something
nuance: Separable; especially British English. Can involve a tricky question or an unexpected situation, not necessarily deliberate deception.

meaning: Empty a space or container and clean its inside.
easyEnglish: Empty a space or container and clean its inside.
japanese: 中身を取り出して、内部をきれいにする。
cue: Your fridge has a strange smell. Suggest a weekend task.
reply: Let's clean out the fridge before we buy more food.
transferCue: A friend asks why the car looks so tidy.
transferReply: I cleaned it out after our camping trip.
frame: Clean something out / clean it out
nuance: Separable. Focuses on the inside and removing contents; clean up is a more general expression for making things tidy.

meaning: Move closer, often from several directions.
easyEnglish: Move closer, often from several directions.
japanese: 周囲から徐々に近づいてくる。
cue: In a game, your group is being surrounded. Warn your teammates.
reply: The other team is closing in on us from both sides.
transferCue: Describe a scene from a wildlife documentary.
transferReply: The wolves waited until dusk before closing in.
frame: Close in / close in on someone
nuance: No direct object. On introduces the target. Often suggests pressure or danger, rather than an ordinary friendly approach.

meaning: Do gentle movement after harder exercise.
easyEnglish: Do gentle movement after harder exercise.
japanese: 運動のあと、軽く体を動かして徐々に落ち着かせる。
cue: You have finished a dance class. Tell a friend why you are still walking around.
reply: I'm taking a few minutes to cool down after the class.
transferCue: Your running partner wants to stop abruptly at the finish. Suggest a gentler ending.
transferReply: Let's walk a little to cool down.
frame: Cool down / cool down after exercise
nuance: Intransitive in this exercise sense. Cooling down can also refer to temperature or anger in other contexts.

meaning: Arrive or develop so gradually that someone is surprised by it.
easyEnglish: Arrive or develop so gradually that someone is surprised by it.
japanese: 気づかないうちに徐々に迫る。
cue: You thought the project deadline was far away. Explain your surprise.
reply: The deadline has crept up on me this month.
transferCue: A friend asks why you suddenly stopped concentrating after a busy day.
transferReply: The tiredness crept up on me during the journey home.
nuance: Keep the person after on. This figurative sense is gradual and unnoticed; the literal sense is approaching quietly.

meaning: Mark an item on a list as finished or no longer needed.
easyEnglish: Mark an item on a list as finished or no longer needed.
japanese: リストの項目を線で消す。
cue: You have booked your accommodation. Update your travel checklist.
reply: We can cross accommodation off the list now.
transferCue: Your friend has already bought the bread. Respond.
transferReply: Thanks, I'll cross it off my shopping list.
frame: Cross something off a list / cross it off
nuance: Separable. Usually removes a listed item from consideration; cross out can also remove an error in ordinary text.

meaning: Become quieter or weaker until it disappears.
easyEnglish: Become quieter or weaker until it disappears.
japanese: 音などが次第に弱まり、消える。
cue: Describe the end of a concert after the musicians left.
reply: The applause slowly died away as people reached for their coats.
transferCue: A noisy motorbike has passed your window. Describe what you hear.
transferReply: I can hear the engine dying away in the distance.
nuance: No direct object. Especially useful for sounds fading into the distance; die out often describes complete disappearance of a custom or species.

meaning: Share a room or other space with another person.
easyEnglish: Share a room or other space with another person.
japanese: 部屋などを二人で共用する。
cue: There are fewer bedrooms than guests at a cabin. Suggest an arrangement.
reply: Two of us will need to double up in the small bedroom.
transferCue: A colleague asks how you managed with too few workstations.
transferReply: We doubled up at the desks until the new office opened.
frame: Double up / double up with someone
nuance: In this sense, people share limited space. Double up with laughter is a different sense involving bending forward.

meaning: Make something last longer than necessary.
easyEnglish: Make something last longer than necessary.
japanese: 必要以上に長引かせる。
cue: A discussion keeps returning to a settled point. Ask to finish.
reply: Let's not drag out the meeting over a decision we've already made.
transferCue: A friend asks why a simple repair took weeks.
transferReply: The repeated requests for photos dragged it out.
frame: Drag something out / drag it out
nuance: Separable. Usually expresses frustration about an unnecessarily long process; drag on describes the process itself continuing.

meaning: Keep thinking or talking about something, often something upsetting.
easyEnglish: Keep thinking or talking about something, often something upsetting.
japanese: 嫌なことなどを繰り返し考えたり話したりする。
cue: You made one mistake in an otherwise good presentation. Describe your reaction.
reply: I keep dwelling on the one slide I got wrong.
transferCue: A friend asks why your project review was so short.
transferReply: We discussed what to change without dwelling on who was to blame.
frame: Dwell on something / dwell on it
nuance: The object follows on. Often suggests excessive attention to a negative topic, rather than useful reflection.

meaning: Start a new activity or situation gradually and gently.
easyEnglish: Start a new activity or situation gradually and gently.
japanese: 新しい活動や状況に少しずつ慣れていく。
cue: You are returning to work after a long break. Explain your plan.
reply: I'll ease into the routine with shorter days at first.
transferCue: A friend is nervous about joining a reading group. Suggest a gentle start.
transferReply: You can ease into it by listening at the first meeting.
frame: Ease into something / ease into doing something
nuance: Keep the activity after into. Emphasizes a gradual transition, rather than starting at full intensity.

meaning: Encourage someone to do something foolish or risky.
easyEnglish: Encourage someone to do something foolish or risky.
japanese: 人をそそのかして、軽率なことをさせる。
cue: Friends are encouraging someone to send an angry message. Object.
reply: Don't egg her on; she might regret sending it.
transferCue: Explain why a harmless prank became a problem.
transferReply: The crowd kept egging him on, and he went too far.
frame: Egg someone on / egg them on
nuance: Separable. Usually disapproving; it is not a neutral replacement for encourage.

meaning: Use a backup when your first plan fails.
easyEnglish: Use a backup when your first plan fails.
japanese: 他の方法がうまくいかないときに頼る。
cue: You are planning an outdoor lunch and rain is possible.
reply: We have the community hall to fall back on if it rains.
transferCue: Your usual tutor is unavailable. Explain your alternative.
transferReply: I can fall back on the recorded lessons this week.
frame: Fall back on something / fall back on it
nuance: Keep all three words together. The object is a reserve source of help or an alternative.

meaning: Lose balance and fall to the ground or onto one side.
easyEnglish: Lose balance and fall to the ground or onto one side.
japanese: バランスを崩して倒れる。
cue: A tall pile of boxes is wobbling. Warn your friend.
reply: Those boxes could fall over if we add another one.
transferCue: Explain the mud on your coat after a walk.
transferReply: I slipped on the path and fell over.
nuance: No direct object. Knock something over means cause it to fall; fall over describes what happens to it.

meaning: Fail to keep up with the work or payments you need to complete.
easyEnglish: Fail to keep up with the work or payments you need to complete.
japanese: 作業や支払いが遅れる。
cue: You missed two classes and need help with homework.
reply: I've got behind with the assignments. Could we review the first one?
transferCue: Tell a colleague why you need a quiet afternoon.
transferReply: I'm getting behind on my emails and need time to catch up.
nuance: With and on introduce the work or payments. Get behind a person can instead mean support them.

meaning: Eat food very quickly.
easyEnglish: Eat food very quickly.
japanese: 食べ物を急いで平らげる。
cue: Your brother ate the snacks before the guests arrived. Describe what happened.
reply: He gobbled up the last of the crackers before anyone noticed.
transferCue: A friend rushes through lunch to reach a train. Comment gently.
transferReply: You don't need to gobble it up; the next train is only ten minutes later.
frame: Gobble something up / gobble it up
nuance: Separable and informal. Often suggests eating too quickly; it can sound playful when describing a pet.

meaning: Follow a plan, rule or agreed limit.
easyEnglish: Follow a plan, rule or agreed limit.
japanese: 計画や決まりから外れずに進める。
cue: Your group keeps adding expensive activities to a trip. Remind them of the budget.
reply: We need to keep to the budget we agreed on.
transferCue: A meeting is running late. Ask to focus on the planned topics.
transferReply: Could we keep to the agenda for the remaining ten minutes?
frame: Keep to something / keep to it
nuance: The object follows to. Keep something to yourself means not share it, which is a different pattern.

meaning: Force someone to leave a place or group.
easyEnglish: Force someone to leave a place or group.
japanese: 人を場所や集団から追い出す。
cue: A player repeatedly insults other members of your game group. Explain the consequence.
reply: They'll kick him out if he keeps insulting people.
transferCue: A friend asks why some visitors left the concert early.
transferReply: Security kicked them out for throwing bottles.
frame: Kick someone out / kick them out of a place
nuance: Separable and informal. Stronger and more blunt than ask someone to leave; it does not require a literal kick.

meaning: Hit or bump something and make it fall.
easyEnglish: Hit or bump something and make it fall.
japanese: 何かに当たって倒す。
cue: Your bag is close to a vase. Warn a friend moving it.
reply: Careful, you might knock over the vase with that bag.
transferCue: Explain the water on the table.
transferReply: I knocked my glass over while reaching for the bread.
frame: Knock something over / knock it over
nuance: Separable. The object falls because something hits it. With a person, this can describe a collision or injury.

meaning: State rules or conditions that people must follow.
easyEnglish: State rules or conditions that people must follow.
japanese: 規則や条件をはっきり定める。
cue: Your team needs clear rules for shared equipment. Suggest an action.
reply: We should lay down a few rules before everyone starts using it.
transferCue: Explain why your group agreed on limits at the start.
transferReply: We laid down the conditions together so there would be no surprises.
frame: Lay down rules / lay something down
nuance: Separable. Fairly firm, often used for authority or agreements. Lay is transitive; lie down means recline.

meaning: Reveal something that you know or have been hiding.
easyEnglish: Reveal something that you know or have been hiding.
japanese: 知っていることや秘密を明かす。
cue: You know about a surprise visit. Ask your friend to keep it secret.
reply: Don't let on that Maya is coming this weekend.
transferCue: Describe how a quiet colleague surprised you with their skill.
transferReply: He knew far more about photography than he let on.
frame: Let on / let on that something is true
nuance: Often used in negatives or comparisons. Do not place a simple noun directly after on in this pattern.

meaning: Use a particular amount or source of money for everyday needs.
easyEnglish: Use a particular amount or source of money for everyday needs.
japanese: ある金額や収入で生活する。
cue: You are considering reducing your working hours. Explain your main concern.
reply: I'm not sure I can live on the lower salary.
transferCue: A friend asks how you managed while changing jobs.
transferReply: I lived on my savings for a couple of months.
frame: Live on an amount / live on savings
nuance: The money follows on. Live on pasta instead describes food someone eats regularly; live off a person stresses dependence.

meaning: Visit someone briefly, often to check how they are.
easyEnglish: Visit someone briefly, often to check how they are.
japanese: 短い間、様子を見に立ち寄る。
cue: Your neighbor is recovering at home. Offer a short visit.
reply: I can look in on you after I collect the children.
transferCue: A colleague asks whether the evening team needs anything.
transferReply: I'll look in before I leave and ask them.
frame: Look in / look in on someone
nuance: Especially British English. On introduces the person; without context, look in a box can simply mean look inside it.

meaning: Handle or change something in a careless or unwanted way.
easyEnglish: Handle or change something in a careless or unwanted way.
japanese: 物をむやみにいじる。
cue: Someone is changing a projector that already works. Ask them to stop.
reply: Please don't mess with the settings; I've just adjusted the colors.
transferCue: Explain why your headphones no longer connect.
transferReply: I messed with the controls and changed the connection mode.
frame: Mess with something / mess with it
nuance: Informal. This lesson concerns interfering with objects; mess with a person can mean provoke or deceive them.

meaning: Admit that you did something wrong.
easyEnglish: Admit that you did something wrong.
japanese: 自分の過ちを認める。
cue: You accidentally deleted a shared note. Tell a colleague what you will do.
reply: I need to own up and explain that I deleted it.
transferCue: Praise a friend who admitted a mistake quickly.
transferReply: Thanks for owning up to the mix-up instead of blaming someone else.
frame: Own up / own up to doing something
nuance: To takes a noun or -ing form. Usually concerns responsibility for something wrong, not ownership of an object.

meaning: Finally pay money that you owe, often after being asked repeatedly.
easyEnglish: Finally pay money that you owe, often after being asked repeatedly.
japanese: 支払うべきお金を、渋々または催促されて払う。
cue: Someone has ignored several reminders about a shared bill. Explain the situation.
reply: He still hasn't paid up, so I'll send one more reminder.
transferCue: A friend asks whether the customer eventually paid you.
transferReply: They paid up after I sent the signed agreement.
nuance: Informal and potentially confrontational as a direct command. A polite payment request is usually better for a customer.

meaning: Continue with determination despite difficulty.
easyEnglish: Continue with determination despite difficulty.
japanese: 困難があっても、決めたことを進める。
cue: Your team lost time fixing a mistake. Encourage them to continue.
reply: We've fixed the problem, so let's press on with the draft.
transferCue: Describe how you finished a long walk before dark.
transferReply: We took a short break and then pressed on toward the village.
frame: Press on / press on with something
nuance: No direct object. Press something on someone means insist that they accept it, a separate pattern.

meaning: Reduce your involvement in something you had planned or started.
easyEnglish: Reduce your involvement in something you had planned or started.
japanese: 関わりや活動を縮小する。
cue: Your group planned too many events. Suggest doing less.
reply: We should pull back from the bigger events until we have more help.
transferCue: A friend asks why your business is advertising less.
transferReply: We've pulled back on paid ads while we improve the website.
frame: Pull back from something / pull back on spending
nuance: From introduces an activity you retreat from; on often introduces spending or another activity you reduce. Physical movement backward is another sense.

meaning: Persuade someone to join an activity or help you.
easyEnglish: Persuade someone to join an activity or help you.
japanese: 人を誘い込んで、手伝ってもらう。
cue: You need extra volunteers to carry tables. Suggest asking friends.
reply: Could we rope in a few friends to help on Saturday?
transferCue: Explain how you ended up helping at a local festival.
transferReply: My neighbor roped me in to run the ticket desk.
frame: Rope someone in / rope them in to help
nuance: Separable and informal. Can imply the person was not initially planning to join; do not use it for a formal invitation.

meaning: Change a number to a simpler number that is lower.
easyEnglish: Change a number to a simpler number that is lower.
japanese: 数値を切り下げて、端数の少ない数にする。
cue: A rough report does not need cents. Explain how you will record 48.70.
reply: I'll round it down to 48 for this rough estimate.
transferCue: A colleague wants a conservative count of available seats.
transferReply: Let's round down to the nearest ten when we estimate capacity.
frame: Round a number down / round down to something
nuance: Separable. Always moves downward; it is different from rounding to the nearest value, which may go up.

meaning: Meet a difficulty that stops or slows your progress.
easyEnglish: Meet a difficulty that stops or slows your progress.
japanese: 予期しない困難や反対にぶつかる。
cue: You cannot finish an online application. Explain the obstacle.
reply: I've run up against a problem with the address form.
transferCue: Describe why your plan for a shared office was delayed.
transferReply: We ran up against opposition from the building owner.
nuance: Keep the problem after against. Unlike run into a friend, this usually describes an obstacle, not a chance meeting.

meaning: Complete something difficult with surprising ease.
easyEnglish: Complete something difficult with surprising ease.
japanese: 試験や難しいことを難なくこなす。
cue: Your friend passed a test they had worried about. Congratulate them.
reply: You sailed through the interview after all that practice.
transferCue: Explain why you were surprised by a difficult second stage.
transferReply: I sailed through the first round, but the next one took much more work.
frame: Sail through something / sail through it
nuance: The object follows through. Often used for tests or checks; it describes ease, not a guarantee that future tasks will be easy.

meaning: Sell unwanted stock or assets, often to raise money or clear space.
easyEnglish: Sell unwanted stock or assets, often to raise money or clear space.
japanese: 不要な在庫や資産などを処分するために売る。
cue: A shop is closing one branch. Explain the discounts.
reply: They're selling off the display furniture before the move.
transferCue: Your club needs money for repairs. Suggest an option.
transferReply: We could sell off the equipment we no longer use.
frame: Sell something off / sell it off
nuance: Separable. Suggests disposal of existing stock or assets; sell out means there is none left to buy.

meaning: Return something to the person or place it came from.
easyEnglish: Return something to the person or place it came from.
japanese: 届いた品物などを送り返す。
cue: A package contains a broken lamp. Explain your next step.
reply: I'll send it back and ask for a replacement.
transferCue: A friend asks whether you kept a jacket bought online.
transferReply: I sent the jacket back because the sleeves were too short.
frame: Send something back / send it back to someone
nuance: Separable. Often used for unsuitable purchases; a return policy may determine whether postage is covered.

meaning: Compare prices and choices before deciding what to buy.
easyEnglish: Compare prices and choices before deciding what to buy.
japanese: 購入前に複数の店やサービスを比べる。
cue: A friend is about to buy the first laptop they see. Suggest comparing options.
reply: It might be worth shopping around before you decide.
transferCue: Explain how you found a better bicycle repair quote.
transferReply: I shopped around and found a smaller shop near the station.
frame: Shop around / shop around for something
nuance: No direct object. For introduces what you want; it can include comparing services and online offers.

meaning: Prevent someone from joining or taking part.
easyEnglish: Prevent someone from joining or taking part.
japanese: 人を話し合いや活動に加えない。
cue: A new colleague feels excluded from decisions. Ask the team to include them.
reply: We shouldn't shut her out of discussions about her own work.
transferCue: Describe how a group conversation made you feel.
transferReply: I felt shut out because everyone kept switching to topics I didn't know.
frame: Shut someone out / shut them out of something
nuance: Separable. Often passive for exclusion. Physically keeping someone outside and blocking noise are other senses.

meaning: Examine someone or something to form a judgment.
easyEnglish: Examine someone or something to form a judgment.
japanese: 人や状況を見て、判断する。
cue: You have just arrived at a crowded event. Explain why you are pausing.
reply: Let me size up the room before we choose where to put the table.
transferCue: Describe your approach to an unfamiliar project.
transferReply: I spent the first morning sizing up the situation and asking questions.
frame: Size someone or something up / size it up
nuance: Separable and conversational. It means assess, not measure clothing size; using it about people can sound judgmental.

meaning: Remove a piece of clothing quickly and roughly.
easyEnglish: Remove a piece of clothing quickly and roughly.
japanese: 服などを急いで脱ぐ。
cue: You came home soaked in the rain. Describe what you did first.
reply: I tore off my wet jacket and reached for a towel.
transferCue: A performer is late for a costume change. Describe the rush backstage.
transferReply: She tore the cape off as soon as she left the stage.
frame: Tear something off / tear it off
nuance: Separable. Tear here rhymes with care and has the forms tore and torn. The garment does not have to be damaged.

meaning: Land after flying.
easyEnglish: Land after flying.
japanese: 飛行機などが着陸する。
cue: Tell the person meeting you when your flight is expected to land.
reply: We should touch down just after lunch.
transferCue: You have arrived but are still on the plane. Send a brief update.
transferReply: We've touched down, but we haven't reached the gate yet.
frame: An aircraft touches down / we touch down
nuance: No direct object in this flight sense. Landing and arriving at the gate happen at different times.

meaning: Persuade someone to support an idea they were unsure about.
easyEnglish: Persuade someone to support an idea they were unsure about.
japanese: 反対や迷いのある人を説得し、支持を得る。
cue: Your neighbors doubt a plan for a shared garden. Suggest a helpful next step.
reply: A small trial might win them over.
transferCue: Explain why you finally agreed to try a new class.
transferReply: The teacher won me over by letting me watch a session first.
frame: Win someone over / win them over
nuance: Separable. Often implies a change from doubt or opposition. Win someone round is a British variant.

meaning: Stay where you are until someone or something arrives or happens.
easyEnglish: Stay where you are until someone or something arrives or happens.
japanese: 人や物事が来る・起こるまで待つ。
cue: Your friend is still getting ready and you are already at the door. Reassure them.
reply: Take your time. I'll wait for you downstairs.
transferCue: Explain why you are standing outside the café instead of going in.
transferReply: I'm waiting for a friend who's running a few minutes late.
frame: Wait for someone / wait for the bus
nuance: Keep for before the person or thing: wait for me, not wait me. Wait for someone to do something adds the action you expect.

meaning: Say that you would like someone to give you something.
easyEnglish: Say that you would like someone to give you something.
japanese: 何かをくださいと頼む。
cue: The menu has no prices for the specials. Tell your friend what you will do.
reply: I'll ask for the prices before we order.
transferCue: A new colleague seems stuck but has not said anything. Encourage them.
transferReply: Don't be afraid to ask for help. Everyone does at first.
frame: Ask for something / ask someone for something
nuance: Put the person before for when you name them: ask the waiter for water. Ask for often introduces a request for help, directions or information.

meaning: Do part of someone's work or give practical help when it is needed.
easyEnglish: Do part of someone's work or give practical help when it is needed.
japanese: 困っている人の作業や用事を手伝う。
cue: A neighbor is carrying boxes up the stairs alone. Offer help.
reply: Do you want me to help out with those boxes?
transferCue: Explain why you spent Saturday at your cousin's shop.
transferReply: Their assistant was ill, so I helped out behind the counter.
frame: Help out / help someone out with something
nuance: Separable: help her out. Out suggests practical support during a busy or difficult time rather than teaching someone.

meaning: Return something to the person who gave it to you.
easyEnglish: Return something to the person who gave it to you.
japanese: 受け取った物を相手に返す。
cue: You borrowed a pen from a classmate to sign a form. Return it.
reply: Thanks, I'll hand it back as soon as I've signed.
transferCue: A teacher explains when students will receive their marked tests.
transferReply: I'll hand the tests back on Thursday.
frame: Hand something back / hand it back
nuance: Separable: hand it back, hand the keys back. Often about things that were only borrowed or collected briefly.

meaning: Make food or drink hot again.
easyEnglish: Make food or drink hot again.
japanese: 料理や飲み物を温め直す。
cue: You got home late and there is leftover curry in the fridge. Say what you will do.
reply: I'll just heat up the curry from yesterday.
transferCue: A guest's coffee has gone cold. Offer to fix it.
transferReply: Your coffee's gone cold. Shall I heat it up for you?
frame: Heat something up / heat it up
nuance: Separable: heat it up. Warm up is a close alternative; heat up suggests making something properly hot. A situation can also heat up, meaning become more intense.

meaning: Go faster, or make something happen faster.
easyEnglish: Go faster, or make something happen faster.
japanese: 速度を上げる。物事を早める。
cue: The film is about to start and you are walking slowly. Tell your friend.
reply: We need to speed up or we'll miss the beginning.
transferCue: Explain how a new online form has changed the sign-up process.
transferReply: The new form speeds up the whole process by a few days.
nuance: Works with or without an object: traffic speeds up; we speeded the process up. The past form can be sped or speeded. Slow down is the opposite.

meaning: Move the text on a screen so that you can see the part below.
easyEnglish: Move the text on a screen so that you can see the part below.
japanese: 画面を下に送って、続きを表示する。
cue: A friend cannot find the Send button on a web form. Help them.
reply: Scroll down a bit. The button is at the bottom of the page.
transferCue: Tell a colleague where to find the latest comments in a shared document.
transferReply: If you scroll down to the last section, you'll see the newest comments.
frame: Scroll down / scroll down to something
nuance: No object in this sense; scroll up moves the other way. Down describes the direction the view moves, not physical movement.

meaning: Change a view so that things look smaller and you see a wider area.
easyEnglish: Change a view so that things look smaller and you see a wider area.
japanese: 表示を縮小して、広い範囲を見る。
cue: A friend is lost in a map app and can only see one street. Suggest a fix.
reply: Zoom out so you can see where the station is.
transferCue: You want the team to stop discussing details and consider the whole plan.
transferReply: Let's zoom out for a minute and look at the whole quarter.
frame: Zoom out / zoom out on a map
nuance: Usually no object: zoom out on the map. The figurative use, stepping back to see the bigger picture, is common in work talk. Zoom in is the opposite.

meaning: Stay the night at someone else's home.
easyEnglish: Stay the night at someone else's home.
japanese: 人の家に泊まる。
cue: Your child asks to stay at a friend's house tonight. Give your answer.
reply: You can sleep over as long as their parents are happy with it.
transferCue: The last train has gone. Offer a friend a place to stay.
transferReply: Why don't you sleep over? The sofa is comfortable.
