nuance: No object: sleep over at a friend's place. A sleepover is the noun, mainly for children's visits. Stay over is a neutral alternative.

meaning: Wash quickly and tidy yourself so you feel clean and comfortable.
easyEnglish: Wash quickly and tidy yourself so you feel clean and comfortable.
japanese: 顔を洗ったり身なりを整えたりして、さっぱりする。
cue: Guests have arrived after a long drive. Show them where the bathroom is.
reply: The bathroom is upstairs if you'd like to freshen up before dinner.
transferCue: You have five minutes between the flight and a meeting. Say what you need.
transferReply: Give me five minutes to freshen up, and then I'm ready.
frame: Freshen up / freshen up before something
nuance: Usually no object when it means washing yourself. Freshen something up can also mean make a room or design look newer.

meaning: Complete the last part of something, or eat or use the last of it.
easyEnglish: Complete the last part of something, or eat or use the last of it.
japanese: 最後の部分を仕上げる。残りを食べきる・使いきる。
cue: There is one slice of pizza left and nobody is taking it. Offer it.
reply: Does anyone want to finish off the pizza?
transferCue: Explain what you will do before leaving the office today.
transferReply: I just need to finish off this report, and then I'm heading home.
frame: Finish something off / finish it off
nuance: Separable: finish it off. Off adds the idea of the very last part. Polish off is a more informal way to say eat all of it.

meaning: Look through a number of things to find what you need or to organize them.
easyEnglish: Look through a number of things to find what you need or to organize them.
japanese: 物や書類を一つずつ確認して整理する。
cue: Your desk drawer is full of old receipts and cables. Say what you plan to do.
reply: I'm going to sort through this drawer and throw most of it away.
transferCue: A colleague asks why you are late replying to messages after your holiday.
transferReply: I'm still sorting through two weeks of emails.
nuance: Inseparable: sort through the papers. Through suggests going from one item to the next. Sort out focuses on the result of putting things in order.

meaning: Fall onto one side, or make something fall onto its side.
easyEnglish: Fall onto one side, or make something fall onto its side.
japanese: 倒れる。倒す。
cue: A tall plant pot on the balcony fell during the storm. Describe what happened.
reply: The wind was so strong that the plant pot tipped over.
transferCue: Warn a child who is leaning back on a chair.
transferReply: Careful, you'll tip the chair over.
nuance: Works with or without an object: the vase tipped over; he tipped it over. Knock over means hit something so that it falls.

meaning: Stay until the end of something long or boring.
easyEnglish: Stay until the end of something long or boring.
japanese: 長くて退屈なものを最後まで我慢して聞く・見る。
cue: A friend asks about the three-hour ceremony you attended. Be honest.
reply: It was nice, but I had to sit through a lot of speeches.
transferCue: Explain why you would rather not go to a particular kind of film.
transferReply: I can't sit through a film that long without a break.
nuance: Inseparable: sit through the meeting. Usually implies patience or mild suffering, so avoid it when praising an event.

meaning: Spend time improving or making something.
easyEnglish: Spend time improving or making something.
japanese: 〜に取り組む。改善のために時間を使う。
cue: Your manager asks what you are doing this afternoon.
reply: I'm working on the slides for Thursday's presentation.
transferCue: A friend asks how your English is going. Mention a weak point.
transferReply: My listening is fine, but I need to work on speaking.
frame: Work on something / work on doing something
nuance: Inseparable: work on the plan, not work the plan on. It describes ongoing effort; work out describes a solution or result.

meaning: Write something quickly so that you remember it.
easyEnglish: Write something quickly so that you remember it.
japanese: 忘れないように手早くメモする。
cue: Someone is giving you a phone number over the phone. Ask them to wait.
reply: Hang on, let me jot that down.
transferCue: Describe how you remember ideas that come to you during the day.
transferReply: I jot ideas down in my phone whenever they come to me.
frame: Jot something down / jot it down
nuance: Separable: jot it down. Suggests a quick, informal note. Write down and note down are neutral; jot emphasizes speed.

meaning: Do someone's work while they are away.
easyEnglish: Do someone's work while they are away.
japanese: 不在の人の代わりに仕事をする。
cue: You have a dentist appointment during your shift. Ask a colleague for a favor.
reply: Could you cover for me between two and three tomorrow?
transferCue: Explain who will handle your emails during your holiday.
transferReply: Dana is covering for me while I'm away, so please contact her.
nuance: Inseparable: cover for her. Cover for can also mean protect someone by hiding their mistake, so context matters. Fill in for is a close alternative.

meaning: Record the time you arrive at work.
easyEnglish: Record the time you arrive at work.
japanese: 出勤時刻を記録する。
cue: A new colleague does not know what to do when they arrive. Explain the routine.
reply: You clock in at the machine by the door, then head to your desk.
transferCue: Explain why you were early this morning.
transferReply: I clocked in at eight so I could leave early for the concert.
frame: Clock in / clock in at eight
nuance: No object. Clock out or clock off records leaving. Clock on is a British alternative for arriving.

meaning: Start or continue doing something, especially work.
easyEnglish: Start or continue doing something, especially work.
japanese: 作業に取りかかる。中断せずに続ける。
cue: The chat about the weekend has gone on for ten minutes. Bring people back to work.
reply: That sounds fun, but we'd better get on with the agenda.
transferCue: Explain what you did after the phone interruption.
transferReply: I just got on with the cleaning after the call.
frame: Get on with something / get on with it
nuance: Inseparable: get on with it. Often signals that talking or waiting should stop. Get on with someone is a separate sense about relationships.

meaning: Complete what you started or promised.
easyEnglish: Complete what you started or promised.
japanese: 始めたこと・約束したことを最後までやり遂げる。
cue: A team has good ideas but rarely completes them. Name the problem carefully.
reply: The ideas are strong; we just need to follow through on them.
transferCue: Praise a friend who actually did what they said they would.
transferReply: You said you'd call the landlord, and you followed through. Thank you.
frame: Follow through on something / follow through with a plan
nuance: Usually no object: follow through on a promise. A follow-through, with a hyphen, is the noun, including the sports sense of completing a swing.

meaning: Lead a team, project or organization.
easyEnglish: Lead a team, project or organization.
japanese: チームや部門を率いる。
cue: Introduce the colleague who will lead the new project.
reply: Mira will head up the launch team from next month.
transferCue: Describe your role at the volunteer group.
transferReply: I head up the fundraising side, mostly events and grants.
frame: Head something up / head up a team
nuance: Separable: head the team up is possible, but head up the team is more common. Lead is neutral; head up sounds like business or organizational talk.

meaning: Ask for something repeatedly or strongly until it happens.
easyEnglish: Ask for something repeatedly or strongly until it happens.
japanese: 実現するまで強く求める。
cue: Everyone complains about the old laptops, but nobody has asked for new ones. Suggest action.
reply: We should push for new laptops in the next budget.
transferCue: Explain how a residents' group got a crossing built near the school.
transferReply: Parents pushed for the crossing for two years before the council agreed.
nuance: Inseparable: push for change. Suggests effort against resistance. Push back on is the opposite move, resisting a proposal.

meaning: Use knowledge, experience or resources to help you do something.
easyEnglish: Use knowledge, experience or resources to help you do something.
japanese: 知識や経験を活用する。
cue: A colleague worries they are too junior to lead a workshop. Point out their strength.
reply: You can draw on your teaching experience. That's exactly what this needs.
transferCue: Explain how you managed a difficult conversation with a neighbor.
transferReply: I drew on what I learned in the mediation course and stayed calm.
frame: Draw on something / draw on your experience
nuance: Inseparable: draw on your savings. Draw upon is a more formal variant. This is not about drawing pictures.

meaning: Remove the people or things that are not wanted from a group.
easyEnglish: Remove the people or things that are not wanted from a group.
japanese: 不要なもの・不適格なものを取り除く。
cue: You have two hundred job applications and one week. Explain your first step.
reply: The first round will weed out applications that don't meet the basic requirements.
transferCue: Describe how you keep your photo library manageable.
transferReply: Every month I weed out the blurry shots and duplicates.
frame: Weed something out / weed out the weak candidates
nuance: Separable: weed them out. The image is pulling weeds from a garden, so it implies removing what is weaker or unwanted.

meaning: Ask for a job, place or permission officially, usually in writing.
easyEnglish: Ask for a job, place or permission officially, usually in writing.
japanese: 仕事や許可などを正式に申し込む。
cue: A friend asks about your plans now that your course is ending.
reply: I'm going to apply for jobs at a few design studios.
transferCue: Explain what you need before your trip abroad.
transferReply: I still have to apply for a visa, so I should start this week.
frame: Apply for a job / apply for a visa
nuance: Inseparable: apply for the position. Apply to names the organization: apply to the university for a place.

meaning: Arrange something for a date or time, knowing it might change.
easyEnglish: Arrange something for a date or time, knowing it might change.
japanese: 変更の可能性を含めて、仮に予定を入れる。
cue: A client wants a meeting next week, but your schedule is not final. Suggest a date.
reply: Let's pencil in Tuesday at ten, and I'll confirm by Friday.
transferCue: A friend proposes a hiking trip for a weekend you are not sure about.
transferReply: Pencil me in for now. I'll know by the end of the month.
frame: Pencil something in / pencil someone in for a date
nuance: Separable: pencil it in. The image is writing in pencil so it can be erased. Say confirmed or in ink when the date is final.

meaning: Plan something in detail, step by step.
easyEnglish: Plan something in detail, step by step.
japanese: 手順や計画を細かく立てる。
cue: Your manager asks how you will finish a six-week project on time.
reply: I've mapped out each week so we know what has to be done by when.
transferCue: Explain how you prepared for a long cycling trip.
transferReply: We mapped out the route and booked a place to stay each night.
frame: Map something out / map out a plan
nuance: Separable: map it out. Suggests a complete overview, like a map. Plan is neutral; map out emphasizes detail and sequence.

meaning: Make a final decision after considering several options.
easyEnglish: Make a final decision after considering several options.
japanese: いくつかの候補から最終的に決める。
cue: After a long discussion about the venue, announce the decision.
reply: We've settled on the community hall. It's cheaper and closer for everyone.
transferCue: A friend asks whether you have chosen a name for the puppy.
transferReply: We finally settled on Mochi after a week of arguing.
frame: Settle on something / settle on a date
nuance: Inseparable: settle on a plan. Implies the options were compared first. Decide on is a close alternative.

meaning: Do something difficult or unpleasant that you have already agreed to do.
easyEnglish: Do something difficult or unpleasant that you have already agreed to do.
japanese: 気が進まなくても、決めたことを実行する。
cue: A friend is nervous about the surgery they scheduled. Ask gently about their decision.
reply: Are you still planning to go through with the operation?
transferCue: Explain why you sold the flat even though you had doubts.
transferReply: We had doubts, but we went through with the sale because the timing was right.
frame: Go through with something / go through with it
nuance: Inseparable: go through with it. Usually implies hesitation or a cost. Go through alone means experience something difficult.

meaning: Do something unpleasant now so that it is finished.
easyEnglish: Do something unpleasant now so that it is finished.
japanese: 嫌なことを早く済ませてしまう。
cue: You are dreading a difficult phone call. Decide to make it now.
reply: I'll make the call now and get it over with.
transferCue: Suggest taking the dentist appointment first thing in the morning.
transferReply: Let's book it for nine and get the whole thing over with before work.
frame: Get something over with / get it over with
nuance: The object goes between get and over: get it over with, never get over with it. Usually about tasks you are not looking forward to.

meaning: Lose the chance to do or enjoy something.
easyEnglish: Lose the chance to do or enjoy something.
japanese: 良い機会や楽しみを逃す。
cue: Tickets for a concert sell out fast. Encourage a friend to book now.
reply: Book today, or you'll miss out.
transferCue: Explain how you feel about skipping a team dinner.
transferReply: I hate missing out on these dinners, but I have an early flight.
frame: Miss out / miss out on something
nuance: Add on before what you lose: miss out on the fun. British English also uses miss something out to mean leave it out of a list.

meaning: Continue with something instead of changing to something else.
easyEnglish: Continue with something instead of changing to something else.
japanese: 変えずに続ける。
cue: You have tried a new running plan for a month and it is working. Tell a friend.
reply: I'm going to stick with this plan. It's the first one I've kept up.
transferCue: The team suggests switching tools again. Argue for staying.
transferReply: Let's stick with the current tool until the project is finished.
frame: Stick with something / stick with it
nuance: Inseparable: stick with it. Stick to is very close; stick with is slightly more informal and often about people, plans or products.

meaning: Begin again from the beginning.
easyEnglish: Begin again from the beginning.
japanese: 最初からやり直す。
cue: The file you were editing got corrupted. Tell your teammate what happens next.
reply: The file is gone, so I'll have to start over.
transferCue: A friend who moved abroad describes their first months. Show understanding.
transferReply: Starting over in a new country takes real courage.
nuance: Mainly American; British speakers often say start again. Usually no object: let's start over. Do something over focuses on repeating one task.

meaning: Reply to a letter, email or message.
easyEnglish: Reply to a letter, email or message.
japanese: 手紙やメールに返事を書く。
cue: A friend sent you a long email a week ago. Apologize for the delay.
reply: Sorry I didn't write back sooner. It's been a busy week.
transferCue: Explain what happened after you emailed the museum.
transferReply: They wrote back the same day with the opening hours.
frame: Write back / write back to someone
nuance: No object: write back to her. Works for email and messages, not only paper letters. Get back to is a spoken alternative for any kind of reply.

meaning: Phone someone.
easyEnglish: Phone someone.
japanese: 電話をかける。
cue: You have not spoken to your grandmother in weeks. Say what you will do tonight.
reply: I'll call her up tonight and see how she's doing.
transferCue: Describe how a friend solved a problem with a broken order.
transferReply: She just called up the shop and they sent a replacement.
frame: Call someone up / call up a friend
nuance: Separable: call him up. Mainly American; British speakers often say ring up or phone. Call up can also mean order someone to join the army.

meaning: Shout encouragement to someone who is competing or trying hard.
easyEnglish: Shout encouragement to someone who is competing or trying hard.
japanese: 声をかけて応援する。
cue: Your friend is running a marathon on Sunday. Tell them your plan.
reply: We'll be near the finish line to cheer you on.
transferCue: Describe the atmosphere at a school sports day.
transferReply: The parents cheered the kids on from the side of the field.
frame: Cheer someone on / cheer them on
nuance: Separable, and the object usually goes in the middle: cheer her on. Root for expresses support without necessarily being there.

meaning: Help people meet or work as a group.
easyEnglish: Help people meet or work as a group.
japanese: 人々を集める。結びつける。
cue: Explain why you organize a monthly neighborhood dinner.
reply: The dinner brings people together who would never meet otherwise.
transferCue: Describe how a difficult year affected your family.
transferReply: Strangely, that year brought us together more than any holiday did.
frame: Bring people together / bring someone together
nuance: Separable, usually with the object in the middle: bring them together. Can describe events, shared problems or a person who connects others.

meaning: Include someone in a plan or activity.
easyEnglish: Include someone in a plan or activity.
japanese: 計画や活動に自分も加える。参加する。
cue: Friends are planning a weekend camping trip. Say you want to join.
reply: Camping sounds great. Count me in!
transferCue: A colleague is collecting names for a charity run. Respond.
transferReply: You can count me in for the run, but I'll be slow.
frame: Count someone in / count me in
nuance: Almost always with the object in the middle: count me in, count us in. Count me out is the opposite. Informal and friendly.

meaning: Give someone a message or information you received from someone else.
easyEnglish: Give someone a message or information you received from someone else.
japanese: 受け取った伝言や情報を別の人に伝える。
cue: A caller wants to leave a message for your colleague who is out. Respond.
reply: Of course. I'll pass the message on as soon as she's back.
transferCue: Thank a friend for their recommendation and mention what you did with it.
transferReply: Thanks for the tip. I passed it on to my sister, and she loved the place.
frame: Pass something on / pass it on to someone
nuance: Separable: pass it on. Also used for handing down objects or spreading an illness. Pass on can be a gentle word for die, so listen for context.

meaning: Stop hoping that someone or something will succeed or improve.
easyEnglish: Stop hoping that someone or something will succeed or improve.
japanese: うまくいくと期待するのをやめる。見限る。
cue: A friend feels their brother will never change. Respond with care.
reply: I understand, but I don't think you should give up on him yet.
transferCue: Explain why you stopped waiting for a reply from a company.
transferReply: After three emails with no answer, I gave up on them and went elsewhere.
frame: Give up on someone / give up on something
nuance: Inseparable: give up on her. Give up alone means stop trying; give up on adds the person or thing you have lost faith in.

meaning: Work together as a group to deal with a difficult situation.
easyEnglish: Work together as a group to deal with a difficult situation.
japanese: 困難に対して皆で協力する。
cue: The venue cancelled the day before your event. Encourage the team.
reply: If we all pull together, we can still make tomorrow happen.
transferCue: Describe how neighbors responded after the flood.
transferReply: The whole street pulled together to clear the mud from the houses.
frame: Pull together / pull together in a crisis
nuance: No object in this sense. Pull yourself together is different: it means regain control of your emotions.

meaning: Tell someone the truth, especially when it is difficult.
easyEnglish: Tell someone the truth, especially when it is difficult.
japanese: 言いにくいことでも正直に話す。
cue: A colleague keeps hearing vague answers about their contract. They ask you directly. Respond.
reply: I'll level with you: the budget for next year isn't confirmed.
transferCue: Ask a friend to be honest about your cooking.
transferReply: Level with me. Was the sauce too salty?
frame: Level with someone / I'll level with you
nuance: Inseparable: level with her. Informal; it signals honesty about something the listener may not want to hear.

meaning: Feel confident that something is right or that someone can succeed.
easyEnglish: Feel confident that something is right or that someone can succeed.
japanese: 〜の価値や力を信じる。
cue: A friend doubts they can pass the exam. Encourage them.
reply: I believe in you. You've prepared more than anyone I know.
transferCue: Explain why you volunteer at the library.
transferReply: I believe in free access to books for everyone.
frame: Believe in someone / believe in something
nuance: Inseparable: believe in him. Believe someone means accept that what they say is true; believe in someone means trust their ability or character.

meaning: Have a particular opinion about someone or something.
easyEnglish: Have a particular opinion about someone or something.
japanese: 〜についてどう思うか、意見を持つ。
cue: You showed a friend your new apartment. Ask for their opinion.
reply: So, what do you think of the place?
transferCue: Share your opinion of a new colleague.
transferReply: I think very highly of her. She listens before she speaks.
frame: What do you think of…? / think highly of someone
nuance: Inseparable: think of it. Think of also means remember or produce an idea: I can't think of his name. Think about focuses on the process of considering.

meaning: Become interested in an activity or subject.
easyEnglish: Become interested in an activity or subject.
japanese: 趣味や分野にはまる。興味を持ち始める。
cue: A friend notices you talk about podcasts a lot. Explain.
reply: I got into podcasts during my commute, and now I can't stop.
transferCue: Ask a friend how they started climbing.
transferReply: How did you get into climbing? You seem so comfortable on the wall.
frame: Get into something / get into a hobby
nuance: Inseparable: get into it. Also means enter a place or be admitted to a school. Be into something describes the interest once it exists.

meaning: Remember a time or event in the past.
easyEnglish: Remember a time or event in the past.
japanese: 過去を振り返って思い出す。
cue: A friend asks how you chose your career. Begin with a memory.
reply: When I think back, it started with a summer job at a radio station.
transferCue: Help someone remember where they left their keys.
transferReply: Think back to when you came in. Did you go to the kitchen first?
frame: Think back / think back to a time
nuance: No object: think back to last summer. Look back on evaluates a period; think back simply recalls it.

meaning: Consider the advantages and disadvantages carefully before deciding.
easyEnglish: Consider the advantages and disadvantages carefully before deciding.
japanese: 長所と短所をよく比べて検討する。
cue: You have two job offers. Explain why you have not decided yet.
reply: I'm still weighing up the two offers. One pays more, but the other is closer to home.
transferCue: A friend asks whether they should move in with their partner. Avoid a quick answer.
transferReply: Only you can weigh up what matters most, but I'm happy to talk it through.
frame: Weigh something up / weigh up the options
nuance: Separable: weigh it up. Mainly British; American speakers often say weigh. Weigh in means join a discussion with your opinion.

meaning: Become more liked by someone over time.
easyEnglish: Become more liked by someone over time.
japanese: だんだん好きになる。
cue: You disliked your new office at first. Describe how you feel now.
reply: The office has grown on me. I even like the noisy coffee machine.
transferCue: A friend is unsure about a song you recommended. Respond.
transferReply: Give it a few more listens. It grows on you.
frame: Something grows on someone / it grew on me
nuance: The thing being liked is the subject: the city grew on me, not I grew on the city. Inseparable.

meaning: Have an opinion or understanding about something.
easyEnglish: Have an opinion or understanding about something.
japanese: 〜をどう解釈するか、どう思うか。
cue: Your manager sent a short, unclear message. Ask a colleague for their reading.
reply: What do you make of this message from Sam?
transferCue: Describe a strange film you saw last night.
transferReply: I honestly didn't know what to make of the ending.
frame: What do you make of…? / not know what to make of something
nuance: Used mostly in questions and negatives: what do you make of it, I couldn't make anything of it. Make of is not about materials here.

meaning: Avoid something because you feel nervous or unsure about it.
easyEnglish: Avoid something because you feel nervous or unsure about it.
japanese: 気が引けて避ける。
cue: A friend never speaks in meetings. Give feedback kindly.
reply: You have good ideas, so try not to shy away from sharing them.
transferCue: Describe how a company handles bad reviews.
transferReply: They don't shy away from criticism. They reply to every negative review.
frame: Shy away from something / shy away from doing something
nuance: Inseparable: shy away from it. A following verb takes -ing: shy away from asking. Suggests avoidance based on nerves or discomfort.

meaning: Have to deal with a problem or opposition that you did not expect.
easyEnglish: Have to deal with a problem or opposition that you did not expect.
japanese: 予想していなかった問題や反対にぶつかる。
cue: Your project stalled because of a rule nobody knew about. Explain to your manager.
reply: We came up against a licensing rule that nobody had mentioned.
transferCue: A friend is renovating and sounds tired. Ask what went wrong.
transferReply: Did you come up against any problems with the old wiring?
frame: Come up against a problem / come up against opposition
nuance: Inseparable: come up against it. The problem is usually unexpected and blocks progress; the subject is the person or project that meets it.
contrast: Come up against and run up against are close; come across simply means find or meet by chance.

meaning: Have to deal with a difficult problem or a strong opponent.
easyEnglish: Have to deal with a difficult problem or a strong opponent.
japanese: 難しい問題や強い相手に直面している。
cue: Your team has one week for a two-week job. Explain the situation to a new member.
reply: We are up against a very tight deadline, so let's decide what can wait.
transferCue: A friend's small shop competes with a big chain. Describe it.
transferReply: They are up against a chain with a much bigger marketing budget.
frame: Be up against something / know what you are up against
nuance: Use a form of be before up against: we are up against, they were up against. It describes the situation, not an action; the object is the problem, opponent or limit.
contrast: Be up against describes an ongoing situation; come up against describes the moment you meet the problem.

meaning: Tell someone not to do something because it could cause problems.
easyEnglish: Tell someone not to do something because it could cause problems.
japanese: 〜しないほうがよいと助言する。
cue: A colleague wants to email the whole company about a small issue. Give your advice.
reply: I would advise against emailing everyone. A message to the team is enough.
transferCue: Your friend plans to drive through the night after work. Respond.
transferReply: I'd advise against driving tonight. You have been awake since five.
frame: Advise against something / advise against doing something
nuance: A following verb takes -ing: advise against selling. You can also advise someone against something: I advised her against it. Fairly formal; in casual speech people often say I wouldn't.

meaning: Continue to dislike or blame someone because of something they did.
easyEnglish: Continue to dislike or blame someone because of something they did.
japanese: 過去のことを根に持って、相手を悪く思う。
cue: A colleague missed your deadline last month and apologized. Reassure them.
reply: I don't hold it against you. Everyone was overloaded that week.
transferCue: A friend wonders whether their sister is still angry about a comment. Respond.
transferReply: She might hold it against you for a while, but not forever.
frame: Hold something against someone / don't hold it against me
nuance: The object always comes between: hold it against him, not hold against him it. Very often negative: I don't hold it against you.

meaning: Be a disadvantage that makes someone less likely to succeed.
easyEnglish: Be a disadvantage that makes someone less likely to succeed.
japanese: 不利に働く。
cue: A friend worries that a gap in their CV will hurt their job application. Respond honestly.
reply: A short gap shouldn't count against you if you explain what you did.
transferCue: Explain why a candidate was not chosen.
transferReply: Her lack of experience with clients counted against her in the end.
nuance: The disadvantage is the subject and the person is the object: his age counted against him. Inseparable.
contrast: Count against harms someone's chances; count on means rely on.

meaning: Take action to prevent something bad from happening.
easyEnglish: Take action to prevent something bad from happening.
japanese: 悪いことが起きないように用心する。
cue: Explain why your team reviews every payment twice.
reply: We check twice to guard against sending money to the wrong account.
transferCue: A friend asks why you keep your phone in a case at the beach.
transferReply: It guards against sand getting into the ports.
frame: Guard against something / guard against doing something
nuance: Inseparable: guard against it. Often followed by a noun for a risk (fraud, mistakes) or an -ing form. Slightly formal; protect against is close.

meaning: Get rid of someone or something because you no longer want them.
easyEnglish: Get rid of someone or something because you no longer want them.
japanese: 不要になった人や物を切り捨てる。
cue: Describe how a company treated its early staff after it grew.
reply: Once the company grew, it cast aside the people who had built it.
transferCue: Encourage a friend to stop worrying about an old plan that no longer fits.
transferReply: You can cast that plan aside. It was written for a different life.
frame: Cast someone aside / cast old ideas aside
nuance: Separable: cast it aside. Literary and often critical, suggesting that a person or thing was dropped without care. Cast is irregular: cast, cast, cast.
contrast: Cast aside is final and dismissive; put aside or set aside is temporary or careful.

meaning: Refuse to think about a feeling or problem so that you can continue.
easyEnglish: Refuse to think about a feeling or problem so that you can continue.
japanese: 気持ちや問題を脇に押しやって考えないようにする。
cue: Explain how you got through a stressful presentation.
reply: I pushed my nerves aside and focused on the first slide.
transferCue: A friend keeps ignoring a health worry. Respond gently.
transferReply: You keep pushing it aside, but a quick check-up would settle it.
frame: Push something aside / push your doubts aside
nuance: Separable: push it aside. The literal sense, moving something to the side with your hand, is also common. Pushing a person aside can mean removing them from a role.
contrast: Push aside ignores a feeling on purpose; brush aside dismisses someone's idea as unimportant.

meaning: Not discuss something now so that you can deal with another point.
easyEnglish: Not discuss something now so that you can deal with another point.
japanese: その点はひとまず置いておく。
cue: A meeting keeps drifting to the budget. Bring it back to the schedule.
reply: Let's leave the budget aside for now and agree on the dates.
transferCue: Explain how you compare two apartments.
transferReply: Leaving aside the rent, the second flat has much better light.
frame: Leave something aside / leaving aside the cost
nuance: Separable: leave it aside. Leaving aside X often opens a sentence to exclude one factor from a comparison. Mostly British and somewhat formal.
contrast: Leave aside excludes a point from the discussion; put aside can also mean save money or time.

meaning: Move someone away from a group to talk to them privately.
easyEnglish: Move someone away from a group to talk to them privately.
japanese: 人を脇へ呼んで、個別に話す。
cue: A new colleague made a small mistake in front of clients. Describe what you did.
reply: I took him aside afterwards and explained what to do next time.
transferCue: Ask a friend how their coach reacted to a bad game.
transferReply: Did she take you aside, or say it in front of the team?
frame: Take someone aside / take them aside for a quiet word
nuance: The person goes between: take her aside. Usually for a private or sensitive conversation, not for something everyone can hear.

meaning: Remove something you do not want, or make it go away.
easyEnglish: Remove something you do not want, or make it go away.
japanese: 不要なものを処分する。取り除く。
cue: Your friend is moving and has too many things. Suggest a first step.
reply: Start by getting rid of the clothes you haven't worn this year.
transferCue: Explain why you opened the windows.
transferReply: I'm trying to get rid of the smell of paint.
frame: Get rid of something / get rid of it
nuance: Inseparable: get rid of it. Works for objects, smells, problems and, informally, people you want to leave. Very common in speech.
contrast: Get rid of removes anything unwanted; throw away is only for putting objects in the bin.

meaning: Look after someone or something, or deal with a task.
easyEnglish: Look after someone or something, or deal with a task.
japanese: 世話をする。用事を処理する。
cue: A colleague is leaving early and worries about a customer call. Reassure them.
reply: Go ahead. I'll take care of the call at four.
transferCue: Explain who looks after your plants when you travel.
transferReply: My neighbor takes care of the plants while I'm away.
frame: Take care of someone / take care of something
nuance: Inseparable: take care of it. Covers people, pets and plants as well as jobs and problems. Take care! alone is a friendly goodbye.
contrast: Take care of and look after both mean care for; only take care of also means handle a task.

meaning: Laugh at someone or make jokes about them in an unkind way.
easyEnglish: Laugh at someone or make jokes about them in an unkind way.
japanese: からかう。ばかにして笑う。
cue: Your child says classmates laugh at their accent. Respond.
reply: Nobody should make fun of the way you speak. Let's talk to your teacher.
transferCue: Explain why you stopped telling a friend about your hobby.
transferReply: He kept making fun of it, so I stopped mentioning it.
frame: Make fun of someone / make fun of something
nuance: Inseparable: make fun of him. Usually unkind, though friends may make fun of each other gently. Poke fun at is a close, slightly lighter alternative.
contrast: Make fun of targets a person or thing; laugh at can be at a joke as well as at a person.

meaning: Understand something that is confusing or complicated.
easyEnglish: Understand something that is confusing or complicated.
japanese: わかりにくいものを理解する。
cue: You received a long report with unclear numbers. Ask a colleague for help.
reply: Can you help me make sense of these figures? The totals don't match.
transferCue: Describe how you felt on your first day in a new country.
transferReply: It took a week to make sense of the bus system.
frame: Make sense of something / try to make sense of it
nuance: Inseparable: make sense of it. Often with try, help or can't: I can't make sense of this. Without of, make sense means be logical: that makes sense.
contrast: Make sense of is understanding something confusing; figure out is solving a problem by thinking.

meaning: Stop holding something, or stop worrying about something from the past.
easyEnglish: Stop holding something, or stop worrying about something from the past.
japanese: 手を離す。過去のことにこだわるのをやめる。
cue: A friend still talks about an argument from years ago. Encourage them kindly.
reply: Maybe it's time to let go of what she said. It's been three years.
transferCue: Describe teaching a child to ride a bike.
transferReply: I let go of the seat, and she kept pedaling without noticing.
frame: Let go of something / let go of the past
nuance: Inseparable: let go of it. Let go without of also works: let go! Letting someone go can mean ending their employment.
contrast: Let go of releases a grip or a worry; give up stops trying.

meaning: Use an opportunity well, or treat someone unfairly for your own benefit.
easyEnglish: Use an opportunity well, or treat someone unfairly for your own benefit.
japanese: 機会を活用する。人の弱みにつけ込む。
cue: The weather is unusually warm for October. Suggest a plan.
reply: Let's take advantage of the sunshine and eat outside.
transferCue: Warn a friend about a landlord who never returns deposits.
transferReply: He takes advantage of students who don't know their rights.
frame: Take advantage of an opportunity / take advantage of someone
nuance: Inseparable: take advantage of it. With a situation it is positive; with a person it means exploit. Context decides.
contrast: Take advantage of uses an opportunity; make the most of stresses getting everything possible from it.

meaning: Think that someone or something is good or acceptable.
easyEnglish: Think that someone or something is good or acceptable.
japanese: よいと思う。賛成する。
cue: Your parents are unsure about your plan to work abroad. Describe their reaction.
reply: They don't fully approve of the move, but they're trying to be supportive.
transferCue: A colleague asks what you think of the new dress code.
transferReply: I approve of it, honestly. Fewer decisions in the morning.
frame: Approve of something / not approve of someone
nuance: Inseparable: approve of it. Often negative: she doesn't approve of him. Without of, approve means officially accept: the board approved the budget.

meaning: Get rid of something, especially by throwing it away in the correct way.
easyEnglish: Get rid of something, especially by throwing it away in the correct way.
japanese: 適切な方法で処分する。
cue: A new tenant asks what to do with old batteries.
reply: You can dispose of batteries at the supermarket. They have a box by the entrance.
transferCue: Describe what your office does with old computers.
transferReply: A recycling company disposes of them and wipes the data first.
frame: Dispose of something / dispose of it safely
nuance: Inseparable: dispose of it. Formal and common on signs and instructions: dispose of responsibly. In speech people usually say get rid of or throw away.
contrast: Dispose of is formal and correct disposal; get rid of is the everyday phrase.

meaning: Continue to know what is happening to something or where it is.
easyEnglish: Continue to know what is happening to something or where it is.
japanese: 〜を把握し続ける。記録しておく。
cue: A colleague asks how you remember all your expenses.
reply: I keep track of them in a spreadsheet and update it every Friday.
transferCue: Explain why you set a timer while cooking.
transferReply: It's hard to keep track of time when I'm on the phone.
frame: Keep track of something / lose track of time
nuance: Inseparable: keep track of it. The opposite is lose track of: I lost track of time. Track is always singular here.
contrast: Keep track of follows something over time; keep an eye on means watch it for problems.

meaning: Avoid someone or something that could cause trouble.
easyEnglish: Avoid someone or something that could cause trouble.
japanese: 面倒を避けるために近づかない。
cue: A colleague asks which topics to avoid at the client dinner.
reply: I'd steer clear of the merger. They're still sensitive about it.
transferCue: Recommend a route to a friend driving into the city.
transferReply: Steer clear of the ring road after five. It's always jammed.
frame: Steer clear of someone / steer clear of a topic
nuance: Inseparable: steer clear of it. Informal and vivid, from steering a boat away from danger. Works for people, places and subjects.
contrast: Steer clear of is deliberate avoidance; stay away from can be a plain instruction.

meaning: Be made up of particular parts or people.
easyEnglish: Be made up of particular parts or people.
japanese: 〜から成る。
cue: Describe your team to a new client.
reply: The team consists of two designers, three developers and me.
transferCue: Explain a simple breakfast.
transferReply: My breakfast usually consists of coffee and whatever fruit is left.
nuance: Inseparable and never passive or continuous: consists of, not is consisting of. The whole is the subject and the parts are the object. Consist in, meaning have as its essence, is rare and formal.
contrast: Consist of lists the parts; be made up of means the same and is a little less formal.

meaning: Be caused by something, or develop from it.
easyEnglish: Be caused by something, or develop from it.
japanese: 〜に起因する。
cue: Explain the real cause of a team's repeated delays.
reply: Most of the delays stem from unclear requirements, not from slow work.
transferCue: Describe why a friend dislikes flying.
transferReply: Her fear stems from a rough landing years ago.
nuance: Inseparable and never passive. The result is the subject and the cause is the object: the problem stems from a mistake. Formal; come from is the everyday version.
contrast: Stem from names the origin of a problem; come down to names the deciding factor.

meaning: Become well again after an illness, or return to normal after a difficult time.
easyEnglish: Become well again after an illness, or return to normal after a difficult time.
japanese: 病気や打撃から回復する。
cue: A colleague asks about your weekend cold.
reply: I'm still recovering from it, but I'll be at the meeting.
transferCue: Describe how a town is doing after a flood.
transferReply: The town is slowly recovering from the flood. Most shops have reopened.
frame: Recover from an illness / recover from a setback
nuance: Inseparable: recover from it. Used for health, shocks and losses; a business or economy can also recover from a bad year. Get over is the informal version.
contrast: Recover from is neutral and medical; get over is informal and also covers ending a bad feeling.

meaning: Stop yourself from doing something, especially something you want to do.
easyEnglish: Stop yourself from doing something, especially something you want to do.
japanese: 〜するのを控える。
cue: Ask meeting attendees not to use their phones, politely and formally.
reply: Please refrain from using your phones during the presentation.
transferCue: Describe how you handled an argument online.
transferReply: I refrained from replying. Nothing I wrote would have helped.
frame: Refrain from doing something / please refrain from…
nuance: Always with -ing or a noun: refrain from smoking. Formal, common in announcements and signs; in conversation say don't or hold back.
contrast: Refrain from is a formal request not to act; hold back is informal self-control.

meaning: Be helped by something or get an advantage from it.
easyEnglish: Be helped by something or get an advantage from it.
japanese: 〜から恩恵を受ける。
cue: Your manager asks who should join the training.
reply: The new hires would benefit from it most. The rest of us have done similar courses.
transferCue: Explain why you want a mentor.
transferReply: I'd benefit from talking to someone who has made the same career change.
frame: Benefit from something / benefit from doing something
nuance: Inseparable: benefit from it. Both people and things can benefit: the garden benefited from the rain. British spelling often doubles the t: benefitted.

meaning: See the difference between two similar things or people.
easyEnglish: See the difference between two similar things or people.
japanese: 〜と区別する。見分ける。
cue: You are introduced to twin brothers. Admit your difficulty.
reply: I still can't tell Tom from Jack unless they're wearing name badges.
transferCue: Explain a difficulty with two similar brands.
transferReply: Without the label, I couldn't tell the cheap one from the expensive one.
frame: Tell A from B / can't tell one from the other
nuance: The two things go on either side of from: tell butter from margarine. Almost always with can or can't. Tell apart is the version with no from.
contrast: Tell from separates two similar things; tell apart means the same with both things as one object.

meaning: Not go near someone or something.
easyEnglish: Not go near someone or something.
japanese: 〜に近づかない。
cue: Tell a child about a rule at the pool.
reply: Stay away from the deep end until the lifeguard says it's okay.
transferCue: A friend asks for advice about a gossiping coworker.
transferReply: I'd stay away from her when she starts on someone. It never ends well.
frame: Stay away from something / stay away from someone
nuance: Inseparable: stay away from it. Common as an instruction or warning. Keep away from means the same; stay away without from means not come.
contrast: Stay away from avoids a place or person; steer clear of adds the idea of avoiding trouble.

meaning: Start to experience criticism, pressure or attack.
easyEnglish: Start to experience criticism, pressure or attack.
japanese: 批判や圧力を受け始める。
cue: Explain why the finance team looks stressed.
reply: They've come under pressure to cut costs before the end of the quarter.
transferCue: Describe how a decision was received.
transferReply: The new policy came under fire from parents on the first day.
frame: Come under pressure / come under fire / come under attack
nuance: Inseparable. Learn the fixed nouns: come under pressure, fire, attack, criticism, scrutiny. A separate sense puts something into a category: this comes under maintenance.
contrast: Come under starts pressure or criticism; be under describes it as an ongoing state.

meaning: Belong to a particular group, category or area of responsibility.
easyEnglish: Belong to a particular group, category or area of responsibility.
japanese: 〜の区分・管轄に入る。
cue: A colleague asks who approves travel costs.
reply: Travel falls under Operations, so send the form to Maria.
transferCue: Explain how you sort your inbox.
transferReply: Anything with a deadline falls under Urgent; the rest can wait until Friday.
frame: Something falls under a category / fall under someone's responsibility
nuance: Inseparable and used for classification: falls under, fell under. Fall under someone's spell or influence is a separate sense about being controlled.
contrast: Fall under classifies; come under can classify too but more often means start receiving pressure.

meaning: Have so much work that you cannot deal with it all.
easyEnglish: Have so much work that you cannot deal with it all.
japanese: 仕事に埋もれて手が回らない。
cue: A friend invites you out this week. Decline honestly.
reply: I am snowed under at work this week. Can we try next Thursday?
transferCue: Ask a colleague whether they can take on a task.
transferReply: Are you snowed under, or do you have room for one more report?
frame: Be snowed under with work / be snowed under at the moment
nuance: Always with a form of be: I am snowed under, she was snowed under. Add with for the cause: snowed under with emails. Informal but fine at work.
contrast: Snowed under is the amount of work; swamped is a close synonym; tied up means busy at a particular moment.

meaning: Give in to pressure or stop resisting because it is too hard.
easyEnglish: Give in to pressure or stop resisting because it is too hard.
japanese: 圧力に屈する。
cue: Describe how a colleague handled unfair demands from a client.
reply: She refused to buckle under. She explained the limits and held her ground.
transferCue: Talk about struggling shops in your area.
transferReply: Many small shops buckled under the pressure of higher rents.
frame: Buckle under pressure / refuse to buckle under
nuance: Intransitive or with under the pressure/strain. Buckle alone can mean the same or describe knees or metal bending. Buckle down is unrelated: start working seriously.
contrast: Buckle under gives in; back down withdraws a demand or claim.

meaning: Look at something or someone quickly and then look away.
easyEnglish: Look at something or someone quickly and then look away.
japanese: 〜をちらっと見る。
cue: You were talking to a friend and checked your phone. Apologize.
reply: Sorry, I just glanced at my phone to check the time.
transferCue: Explain how you noticed a mistake in a report so fast.
transferReply: I only glanced at the first page and the date was wrong.
frame: Glance at something / glance at your watch
nuance: Inseparable: glance at it. A glance is quick and often casual; glance through or glance over a document means look at it briefly. Take a glance at is the noun form.
contrast: Glance at is quick; stare at is long and fixed.

meaning: Keep something rather than losing, selling or giving it away.
easyEnglish: Keep something rather than losing, selling or giving it away.
japanese: 手放さずに持っておく。
cue: A friend wants to sell an old guitar for a low price. Give your opinion.
reply: I'd hold on to it. You'll want it again when you have more time.
transferCue: Tell a colleague what to do with the receipt.
transferReply: Hold on to the receipt until the refund arrives.
frame: Hold on to something / hold on to your ticket
nuance: Inseparable: hold on to it. Also spelled hold onto. Without to, hold on means wait. Hang on to means the same and is a little more informal.
contrast: Hold on to keeps something; hold on alone asks someone to wait.

meaning: Laugh because of something funny, or laugh at someone in an unkind way.
easyEnglish: Laugh because of something funny, or laugh at someone in an unkind way.
japanese: 〜を笑う。ばかにして笑う。
cue: Your friend worries that people will laugh if they sing at karaoke. Reassure them.
reply: Nobody is going to laugh at you. Half of us can't sing either.
transferCue: Describe a comedy show you watched.
transferReply: We laughed at every joke, even the ones we had heard before.
frame: Laugh at a joke / laugh at someone
nuance: Inseparable: laugh at it. With a joke or story it is neutral; with a person it is usually unkind. Laugh with someone shares the joke.
contrast: Laugh at can be unkind; make fun of always is.

meaning: Look at someone or something for a long time without moving your eyes.
easyEnglish: Look at someone or something for a long time without moving your eyes.
japanese: 〜をじっと見る。
cue: Describe what you did when your laptop froze before a deadline.
reply: I just stared at the screen for a minute before I remembered to save.
transferCue: A child keeps looking at a stranger's tattoos. Explain quietly.
transferReply: Don't stare at people. You can ask me about it later.
frame: Stare at something / stare at someone
nuance: Inseparable: stare at it. Staring at a person can seem rude in many cultures. Gaze at is softer and admiring; glance at is quick.
contrast: Stare at is long and fixed; look at is neutral.

meaning: Suggest something indirectly without saying it clearly.
easyEnglish: Suggest something indirectly without saying it clearly.
japanese: 〜をほのめかす。
cue: A colleague seems to be hinting about leaving. Describe it to a friend.
reply: She keeps hinting at a new job, but she hasn't said anything directly.
transferCue: Your partner asks what you want for your birthday.
transferReply: I've been hinting at a weekend away for months!
frame: Hint at something / hint at the possibility of…
nuance: Inseparable: hint at it. The object is the thing suggested, not the listener. Hint that + clause is also common: he hinted that he might leave.
contrast: Hint at is deliberately indirect; bring up raises the topic openly.

meaning: Reach a decision, answer or agreement after discussion or thought.
easyEnglish: Reach a decision, answer or agreement after discussion or thought.
japanese: 結論や合意に達する。
cue: Report the outcome of a long negotiation.
reply: After two meetings, we arrived at a price both sides can accept.
transferCue: Explain how you chose your apartment.
transferReply: We arrived at the decision by listing what we couldn't live without.
frame: Arrive at a decision / arrive at a conclusion / arrive at an agreement
nuance: Inseparable: arrive at it. Used with decisions, conclusions, agreements, figures and answers. Arrive in or at a place is the literal use.
contrast: Arrive at emphasizes the process that led to the decision; settle on emphasizes choosing one option.

meaning: Eat only small amounts of food without interest, or keep touching something with your fingers.
easyEnglish: Eat only small amounts of food without interest, or keep touching something with your fingers.
japanese: 食べ物を少しずつつまむ。指でいじる。
cue: A friend hardly touched dinner. Ask if they are okay.
reply: You've been picking at your food all evening. Is everything all right?
transferCue: Tell a child to leave a scab alone.
transferReply: Don't pick at it, or it will take longer to heal.
frame: Pick at your food / pick at a scab
nuance: Inseparable: pick at it. With food it suggests no appetite; with a scab, a loose thread or paint it means keep pulling with your fingers. Pick on is different: treat unfairly.

meaning: Criticize someone angrily, or try to do something.
easyEnglish: Criticize someone angrily, or try to do something.
japanese: 人を非難する。〜を試してみる。
cue: A colleague was harsh with the intern. Describe what happened.
reply: He had a go at the intern for a typo. It was completely out of proportion.
transferCue: Encourage a nervous friend to try climbing.
transferReply: Have a go at the easy wall first. You can always stop.
frame: Have a go at someone (criticize) / have a go at something (try)
nuance: With a person it means criticize, and is British and informal. With an activity it means try: have a go at surfing. Go is a noun here, so have changes: had a go, having a go.
contrast: Have a go at someone attacks them in words; tell off is what a parent or boss does.

meaning: Make arrangements for the future before you need them.
easyEnglish: Make arrangements for the future before you need them.
japanese: 前もって計画を立てる。
cue: A friend always books trains at the last minute and pays more. Advise them.
reply: If you plan ahead and book a month early, the tickets are half the price.
transferCue: Explain how your team avoids end-of-year stress.
transferReply: We plan ahead. The December schedule is fixed by October.
frame: Plan ahead / plan ahead for something
nuance: No object: plan ahead. Add for before the event: plan ahead for the holidays. Think ahead is similar but about thinking rather than arranging.
contrast: Plan ahead arranges things early; think ahead considers what may happen.

meaning: Continue with a plan in a determined way despite problems or opposition.
easyEnglish: Continue with a plan in a determined way despite problems or opposition.
japanese: 反対や困難があっても計画を推し進める。
cue: The client raised doubts, but the deadline has not moved. Tell the team the decision.
reply: We're pressing ahead with the launch. The doubts are noted, and we'll address them in the next version.
transferCue: Describe a council that ignored protests.
transferReply: The council pressed ahead with the new road despite the protests.
frame: Press ahead with something / press ahead despite…
nuance: Intransitive; add with before the plan: press ahead with the changes. Suggests determination and, sometimes, ignoring objections. Press on means the same.
contrast: Press ahead continues with a plan despite objections; go ahead simply starts or proceeds.

meaning: Offer to help or to do something when no one else has.
easyEnglish: Offer to help or to do something when no one else has.
japanese: 進んで申し出る。名乗り出る。
cue: Nobody has volunteered to organize the farewell party. Describe who saved the day.
reply: Nobody wanted to organize it, so Ana stepped forward and did it in two days.
transferCue: Ask a room of neighbours for help with a problem.
transferReply: We need two people to talk to the landlord. Would anyone step forward?
frame: Step forward / step forward to help
nuance: No object. Also literal: take a step to the front. Come forward is close but usually about giving information to the police or an inquiry.
contrast: Step forward volunteers; come forward offers information.

meaning: Remain in a place after other people have left.
easyEnglish: Remain in a place after other people have left.
japanese: 他の人が帰ったあとも残る。
cue: A teacher asks to speak with you after class. Tell a friend why you're late.
reply: I had to stay behind to talk about my essay.
transferCue: Explain what happened after the concert.
transferReply: A few of us stayed behind to help pack up the chairs.
frame: Stay behind / stay behind after class
nuance: No object. Add after for the event: stay behind after the meeting. Remain behind is the formal version; stay on means keep a job or position longer.
contrast: Stay behind is for a short time after others leave; stay on continues in a place or job for longer.

meaning: Move or develop more slowly than others.
easyEnglish: Move or develop more slowly than others.
japanese: 他より遅れる。
cue: Report on a project's progress compared with other teams.
reply: Our documentation is lagging behind the code. The features are ready, but nothing is written up.
transferCue: Describe a runner in a race.
transferReply: She lagged behind for the first lap and then passed everyone on the hill.
frame: Lag behind someone / lag behind in something
nuance: With an object (lag behind the others) or alone. Common in reports about sales, growth and progress. Fall behind is close; lag suggests a continuing slow pace.
contrast: Lag behind is being slower over time; fall behind is failing to keep up with expected progress.

meaning: Stop thinking about a bad experience so that it no longer affects you.
easyEnglish: Stop thinking about a bad experience so that it no longer affects you.
japanese: 嫌な経験を過去のものにする。
cue: A colleague still feels bad about a failed launch last year. Respond.
reply: It's time to put that launch behind you. Everyone has moved on.
transferCue: Describe how a team recovered after a loss.
transferReply: They put the defeat behind them and won the next three games.
frame: Put something behind you / put it behind us
nuance: The experience goes between put and behind, and the pronoun after behind matches the subject: I put it behind me, they put it behind them.
contrast: Put behind you is choosing to move on; get over is recovering emotionally.

meaning: Deal with something that needs attention.
easyEnglish: Deal with something that needs attention.
japanese: 必要なことを処理する。
cue: A guest mentions the tap in the bathroom is dripping. Respond as the host.
reply: Sorry about that. I'll see to it this afternoon.
transferCue: Divide tasks before a party.
transferReply: You see to the drinks, and I'll see to the music.
frame: See to something / I'll see to it
nuance: Inseparable: see to it. Common in offers and promises: I'll see to that. See to it that + clause means make sure: see to it that the door is locked.
contrast: See to deals with a task; look after cares for a person or thing over time.

meaning: Become familiar with something so that it no longer seems strange or difficult.
easyEnglish: Become familiar with something so that it no longer seems strange or difficult.
japanese: 〜に慣れる。
cue: A new colleague finds the early start hard. Encourage them.
reply: You'll get used to the seven o'clock start. It took me about a month.
transferCue: Describe your first weeks driving on the other side of the road.
transferReply: I got used to driving on the left faster than I expected.
frame: Get used to something / get used to doing something
nuance: A following verb takes -ing: get used to waking up early. Be used to describes the finished state; used to + verb, without get or be, means a past habit.
contrast: Get used to is becoming familiar; be used to is already familiar.

meaning: Be the same as something in effect, or add up to a total.
easyEnglish: Be the same as something in effect, or add up to a total.
japanese: 結局〜に等しい。合計で〜になる。
cue: A colleague describes a new proposal as a big change. Give your view.
reply: It amounts to the same plan with a new name.
transferCue: Summarize the cost of small daily purchases.
transferReply: A coffee a day amounts to over a thousand dollars a year.
frame: Something amounts to… / it amounts to the same thing
nuance: Inseparable and never passive. Not amount to much means be unimportant or unsuccessful: the complaints didn't amount to much.
contrast: Amount to says what something really is or totals; add up to is the informal version for totals.

meaning: Do something you would rather not do because there is no other way.
easyEnglish: Do something you would rather not do because there is no other way.
japanese: 他に方法がなく、やむを得ず〜に頼る。
cue: Explain why you finally called a plumber at midnight.
reply: We had to resort to an emergency plumber after the pipe burst.
transferCue: Describe a store's response to falling sales.
transferReply: In the end they resorted to cutting prices, which they had wanted to avoid.
frame: Resort to something / resort to doing something
nuance: A following verb takes -ing: resort to borrowing. Suggests reluctance and a poor option. As a last resort is the related noun phrase.
contrast: Resort to is a reluctant choice; fall back on uses a reserve plan without the negative feeling.

meaning: Be doing something, especially something secret or naughty.
easyEnglish: Be doing something, especially something secret or naughty.
japanese: （こっそり）何かをしている。
cue: You call a friend on Saturday morning. Ask what they're doing.
reply: Hey, what are you up to this weekend?
transferCue: The children have gone very quiet. Comment to your partner.
transferReply: They are up to something. It's never this quiet.
frame: What are you up to? / be up to something / it's up to you
nuance: Always with a form of be: what are you up to, he was up to something. Up to something suggests mischief. It's up to you means you decide, and up to ten means a maximum.
contrast: Be up to asks about activity; be up for asks whether someone wants to do something.

meaning: Be owned by someone, or be a member of a group.
easyEnglish: Be owned by someone, or be a member of a group.
japanese: 〜のものである。〜に所属する。
cue: You find a jacket in the meeting room. Ask around.
reply: Does this jacket belong to anyone here?
transferCue: Tell a new neighbour about local groups.
transferReply: I belong to the running club that meets by the river on Sundays.
frame: Something belongs to someone / belong to a club
nuance: Inseparable and never continuous: it belongs to me, not it is belonging to me. Belong without to means be in the right place: the cups belong in that cupboard.

meaning: Mention or talk about someone or something, or look at a source for information.
easyEnglish: Mention or talk about someone or something, or look at a source for information.
japanese: 〜に言及する。〜を参照する。
cue: Your manager mentioned 'the incident' in a message. Ask what they meant.
reply: When you referred to the incident, did you mean the server outage?
transferCue: Tell a colleague where to find the rules for expenses.
transferReply: Refer to the travel policy on page four before booking.
frame: Refer to something / refer to someone as…
nuance: Inseparable: refer to it. Refer to someone as + name gives what you call them. Refer someone to a specialist is a different pattern: send them.
contrast: Refer to mentions or consults; look up finds a specific piece of information.

meaning: Say that you disagree with or disapprove of something.
easyEnglish: Say that you disagree with or disapprove of something.
japanese: 〜に反対する。異議を唱える。
cue: The team proposes meeting at 8 a.m. Disagree politely.
reply: I'd object to eight o'clock. Half the team drops children at school then.
transferCue: Describe a neighbour's reaction to a new fence.
transferReply: He objected to the fence because it blocks his afternoon light.
frame: Object to something / object to doing something
nuance: A following verb takes -ing: object to paying. The verb is stressed on the second syllable: obJECT. Object alone can introduce speech: 'That's unfair,' she objected.
contrast: Object to is a formal disagreement; push back on is an informal, workplace version.

meaning: Deal with something or find out about it, especially by arranging it.
easyEnglish: Deal with something or find out about it, especially by arranging it.
japanese: 手配のために調べる・対応する。
cue: Your team needs a bigger meeting room next week. Offer to arrange it.
reply: I'll see about booking the large room. Facilities usually needs a day's notice.
transferCue: Your friend asks whether your landlord will fix the heating.
transferReply: I've asked him to see about the boiler before the weekend.
frame: See about something / see about doing something
nuance: Inseparable. A following verb takes -ing: see about getting tickets. We'll see about that! is a warning that you will stop something.
contrast: See about arranges or looks into something; see to promises to deal with it fully.

meaning: Support one person or group in an argument.
easyEnglish: Support one person or group in an argument.
japanese: 口論で一方の味方をする。
cue: Two friends argued about splitting a bill, and one asks whose side you were on.
reply: I didn't want to side with either of you. You both had a point.
transferCue: Describe what happened in a family debate.
transferReply: My brother always sides with Mum, whatever the topic.
frame: Side with someone / side with someone against someone
nuance: Inseparable: side with her. Add against for the other party: he sided with the union against management. Take someone's side means the same.
contrast: Side with supports one party in a dispute; back up supports a claim with evidence.

meaning: Give something away or sell it, especially when you would rather keep it.
easyEnglish: Give something away or sell it, especially when you would rather keep it.
japanese: 惜しみながら手放す。
cue: Explain why you still have your first bicycle.
reply: I can't part with it. My grandfather taught me to ride on it.
transferCue: Talk about clearing a bookshelf.
transferReply: I parted with about fifty books, but the poetry stays.
frame: Part with something / hard to part with
nuance: Inseparable: part with it. Suggests the thing is valued; part with money means spend it unwillingly. Not used for people; part from someone is rare and formal.
contrast: Part with gives up something you value; get rid of removes something you don't want.

meaning: Deal successfully with a difficult situation or a large amount of work.
easyEnglish: Deal successfully with a difficult situation or a large amount of work.
japanese: 困難にうまく対処する。
cue: A friend asks how you handle two young children and a job.
reply: Some weeks I cope with it better than others. A shared calendar helps.
transferCue: Describe a website during a sale.
transferReply: The site couldn't cope with the traffic and went down for an hour.
frame: Cope with something / cope with stress
nuance: Inseparable: cope with it. Cope alone also works: she's coping well. Both people and systems can cope with demands.
contrast: Cope with manages a difficulty; deal with handles a task or person and need not be difficult.

meaning: Be about to experience something, usually something unpleasant.
easyEnglish: Be about to experience something, usually something unpleasant.
japanese: （嫌なことが）待ち受けている。
cue: Look at the forecast and warn a friend about tomorrow's hike.
reply: We are in for a wet morning. Bring the proper jacket.
transferCue: Comment on a colleague who has never worked with a demanding client.
transferReply: She is in for a surprise when she sees his first round of comments.
frame: Be in for something / be in for a shock / be in for a treat
nuance: Always with a form of be. Mostly unpleasant (a shock, a long night), but in for a treat is positive. Different from be in for a job, which means have applied for it.
contrast: Be in for is what will happen to you; be up for is what you want to do.

meaning: Be careful to notice something dangerous or important.
easyEnglish: Be careful to notice something dangerous or important.
japanese: 〜に気をつける。
cue: Give a cycling friend a warning about your street.
reply: Watch out for the tram lines at the corner. They're slippery when wet.
transferCue: Tell a new colleague what to check in customer emails.
transferReply: Watch out for orders with a different billing and delivery address.
frame: Watch out for something / watch out!
nuance: Inseparable: watch out for it. Watch out! alone is an urgent warning. Look out for means the same, and can also mean take care of someone.
contrast: Watch out for warns about danger; look out for can also mean try to notice or protect someone.

meaning: Continue to support someone in a difficult time, or keep to a decision.
easyEnglish: Continue to support someone in a difficult time, or keep to a decision.
japanese: 困難なときも支え続ける。決めたことを守る。
cue: Describe how your friends reacted when you lost your job.
reply: They stuck by me the whole time. Someone called every day.
transferCue: A manager is asked to change a decision under pressure. Describe their answer.
transferReply: She stuck by her decision and explained the reasons again.
frame: Stick by someone / stick by a decision
nuance: Inseparable: stick by her. Stick is irregular: stuck. Stand by means the same for people; stick to is used for rules and plans.
contrast: Stick by supports a person or holds a decision; stick with keeps doing something.

meaning: Stop letting something upset or block you, or manage to pass an obstacle.
easyEnglish: Stop letting something upset or block you, or manage to pass an obstacle.
japanese: 気持ちの上で乗り越える。障害を通り抜ける。
cue: A friend can't stop thinking about a rude comment. Respond.
reply: I know it stung, but try to get past it. He was having a bad day.
transferCue: Explain a difficulty with a job application.
transferReply: I never got past the first interview, so I don't know what they wanted.
frame: Get past something / can't get past the fact that…
nuance: Inseparable: get past it. Often negative: I can't get past what she said. Literal use is also common: we couldn't get past the roadworks.
contrast: Get past stops a thought from blocking you; get over recovers from an upset.

meaning: Believe that someone is capable of doing something bad or surprising.
easyEnglish: Believe that someone is capable of doing something bad or surprising.
japanese: 〜ならやりかねないと思う。
cue: A colleague suspects the new manager will cancel the bonus. Give your view.
reply: I wouldn't put it past him. He cut the travel budget in his first week.
transferCue: Your friend jokes that your cat opened the fridge. Respond.
transferReply: Honestly, I wouldn't put it past her. She has learned to open doors.
frame: Not put it past someone to do something / I wouldn't put it past her
nuance: Almost always negative with would: I wouldn't put it past him. The it stays fixed between put and past, and a following verb takes to: I wouldn't put it past them to cancel.

meaning: Make someone or something different from and better than others.
easyEnglish: Make someone or something different from and better than others.
japanese: 他と際立たせる。
cue: Explain why you chose one candidate over several strong ones.
reply: Her calm under pressure set her apart from the other candidates.
transferCue: Describe what makes your favourite café different.
transferReply: What sets it apart is the owner, who remembers everyone's order.
frame: Set someone apart from others / what sets it apart is…
nuance: Separable, usually with the object between: set her apart. Add from for the group: set apart from the rest. Often positive; a separate sense means reserve time or money.
contrast: Set apart makes something stand out; stand out is what the thing itself does.

meaning: Separate people or things that are together, or criticize something in detail.
easyEnglish: Separate people or things that are together, or criticize something in detail.
japanese: 引き離す。細かく批判する。
cue: Two children are fighting over a toy. Describe what you did.
reply: I had to pull them apart before someone got hurt.
transferCue: Describe how a reviewer treated your draft.
transferReply: She pulled the argument apart paragraph by paragraph, but her notes were fair.
frame: Pull people apart / pull an argument apart
nuance: Separable: pull them apart. With people it is physical separation; with a plan or piece of writing it means find every weakness. Tear apart is stronger and more emotional.
contrast: Pull apart separates or dissects; fall apart is what a thing does when it breaks by itself.

meaning: Make or prepare something quickly and without much care.
easyEnglish: Make or prepare something quickly and without much care.
japanese: 手早く間に合わせで作る。
cue: Unexpected guests arrive at dinner time. Reassure your partner.
reply: I can throw together a pasta with what's in the fridge.
transferCue: Explain why a presentation looked rough.
transferReply: We threw it together the night before, so the slides don't match.
frame: Throw something together / throw a meal together
nuance: Separable: throw it together. Suggests speed and improvisation rather than poor quality. People can also be thrown together by circumstances: we were thrown together on a training course.
contrast: Throw together is fast and improvised; put together is careful assembly.

meaning: Join with other people in order to achieve something together.
easyEnglish: Join with other people in order to achieve something together.
japanese: 力を合わせるために団結する。
cue: Describe how your street dealt with a noisy construction site.
reply: The neighbours banded together and asked the council for quiet hours.
transferCue: Encourage colleagues to respond to a policy as a group.
transferReply: If we band together, they will have to listen. One complaint is easy to ignore.
frame: Band together / band together to do something / band together against something
nuance: No object. Usually a group with a shared problem or goal; add against for an opponent. Join forces means the same in more formal writing.
contrast: Band together is people uniting for a purpose; get together is simply meeting.

meaning: Make fast progress or continue with determination.
easyEnglish: Make fast progress or continue with determination.
japanese: 力強く前進する。
cue: Give a short status update on a project that is going well.
reply: The design team is forging ahead. Two screens are already in testing.
transferCue: Describe a friend who kept studying while others quit.
transferReply: Most of the class dropped out, but she forged ahead and passed in June.
frame: Forge ahead / forge ahead with something
nuance: No object; add with for the project: forge ahead with the plan. Forge is pronounced with a soft g, like large. Slightly literary and positive.
contrast: Forge ahead stresses energetic progress; press ahead stresses continuing despite objections.

meaning: Move in front of others in a race, competition or market.
easyEnglish: Move in front of others in a race, competition or market.
japanese: 競争相手を抜いて先に出る。
cue: Describe how the sales race between two teams changed in March.
reply: Our team pulled ahead in March after the new pricing went live.
transferCue: Talk about a cycling race you watched.
transferReply: She pulled ahead on the final climb and won by twenty seconds.
frame: Pull ahead / pull ahead of someone
nuance: No object; add of for the rival: pull ahead of the competition. From racing, now common in business and sport. Get ahead is about personal success rather than a race.
contrast: Pull ahead overtakes a rival; get ahead advances in life or a career.

meaning: Continue moving or working towards a goal with effort.
easyEnglish: Continue moving or working towards a goal with effort.
japanese: 努力して前に進める。
cue: The first version of a feature got mixed feedback. Tell the team the plan.
reply: The feedback is useful, but we'll push forward with the release and fix the rough edges next sprint.
transferCue: Describe a hike in bad weather.
transferReply: The rain got heavier, but we pushed forward to the hut.
frame: Push forward / push forward with something
nuance: No object in this sense; add with for the plan. Push something forward can also mean move a date or item earlier or higher in priority. Push ahead and press ahead are close.
contrast: Push forward keeps moving despite effort; move on leaves one thing to start the next.

meaning: Have a similar appearance to someone or something, or seem likely.
easyEnglish: Have a similar appearance to someone or something, or seem likely.
japanese: 〜に似ている。〜のようだ。
cue: A friend shows you a photo of their brother. React.
reply: He looks like you, especially the smile.
transferCue: Look at the sky and comment on the weather.
transferReply: It looks like rain. Let's take the umbrella.
frame: Look like someone / it looks like rain / it looks like + clause
nuance: Inseparable: look like her. Followed by a noun, or by a clause in speech: it looks like we're late. What does he look like? asks about appearance; what is he like? asks about character.
contrast: Look like is about appearance or likelihood; feel like is about wanting something.

meaning: Eat a very large amount of food.
easyEnglish: Eat a very large amount of food.
japanese: がつがつ食べる。食べすぎる。
cue: A friend asks what you did on a lazy Sunday.
reply: We pigged out on leftovers and watched three films.
transferCue: Set expectations before a big family dinner.
transferReply: Don't pig out on the bread. There are four more courses.
nuance: Informal and intransitive: on introduces the food. Light and self-deprecating, not for formal writing.

meaning: Follow a rule, plan or agreement exactly.
easyEnglish: Follow a rule, plan or agreement exactly.
japanese: 規則や取り決めを、そのとおり守る。
cue: A contractor asks how strict the site rules are.
reply: Everyone on site has to adhere to the safety procedure.
transferCue: Describe how a club handles its constitution.
transferReply: The committee adheres to the rules even when they're inconvenient.
nuance: Inseparable and formal: adhere to it, never adhere it to. Stick to is the everyday alternative.
contrast: Adhere to is formal about rules; stick to is the everyday version.

meaning: Mention something indirectly.
easyEnglish: Mention something indirectly.
japanese: 直接には言わず、それとなく触れる。
cue: Someone hinted at a problem without naming it. Describe what happened.
reply: She alluded to a disagreement but didn't say who with.
transferCue: Ask a colleague to be clearer.
transferReply: You alluded to a risk earlier. Could you say what it is?
nuance: Inseparable and fairly formal. It always means indirect mention; refer to can be direct.
contrast: Allude to hints at something; refer to names it directly.

meaning: Take responsibility for something and explain it.
easyEnglish: Take responsibility for something and explain it.
japanese: 責任を負って、説明する立場に立つ。
cue: A decision will need explaining at a review. Say who will do it.
reply: I'll answer for the delay. It was my call.
transferCue: Describe accountability in a team.
transferReply: Each lead answers for their own budget.
nuance: Inseparable. Have a lot to answer for is a common critical variant.
contrast: Answer for takes responsibility; account for explains a cause or a total.

meaning: Have a strong wish to achieve something.
easyEnglish: Have a strong wish to achieve something.
japanese: ある目標を、強く目指す。
cue: A colleague asks where you want to be in five years.
reply: I aspire to run a team of my own eventually.
transferCue: Describe what a small organisation wants to become.
transferReply: They aspire to the same standard as the national museums.
frame: Aspire to something / to do something
nuance: Inseparable and formal. Followed by a noun or by to plus a verb.
contrast: Aspire to is a long-term ambition; aim for is about a specific target.
